title: Local IL-17A neutralization reduces experimental peri-implant bone loss in type 2 diabetic rats.
abstract: Background The purpose of this study was to investigate whether local IL-17A neutralization attenuates peri-implant alveolar bone resorption in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) rats. Methods Thirty male Sprague-Dawley rats with T2DM were randomly divided into three groups (n = 10): a control group (without ligature‑induced peri‑implantitis), a peri-implantitis (PI) group, and an anti-IL-17A group. Peri-implant bone changes were evaluated by micro-CT, osteoclastogenesis by TRAP staining, and inflammatory responses by H&E staining, qPCR, immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence. Results Micro-CT revealed significantly greater linear and volumetric bone resorption in the PI group versus controls, which was reduced by IL-17A neutralization. TRAP staining showed increased osteoclasts in the PI group, attenuated by IL-17A neutralization. H&E staining confirmed exacerbated inflammation and bone resorption in the PI group, attenuated by anti-IL-17A. Inflammatory cytokine mRNAs were upregulated in the PI group, with IL-17A exhibiting the most pronounced increase; IL-17A neutralization reduced these levels, with IL-17A showing the greatest reduction-confirmed at the protein level. Immunofluorescence showed increased MPO+ neutrophils, IL-6+cells, and RANKL+ cells in the PI group versus controls, reduced by IL-17A neutralization. Conclusion Our findings demonstrate that local IL-17A blockade effectively attenuates peri-implant alveolar bone resorption in T2DM rats by suppressing inflammatory responses and osteoclastogenesis, supporting this targeted strategy as a promising therapeutic approach for diabetic peri-implantitis. However, as these are preclinical results, further studies are needed to validate the therapeutic relevance of this targeted strategy for diabetic peri‑implantitis.

title: Low-risk paediatric Crohn's disease: A narrative review of current evidence and unmet research needs.
abstract: While current paediatric management increasingly favours early intensive treatment for children and adolescents with Crohn's disease (CD) at high risk of disease progression, a smaller subset of patients presents with a potentially 'low-risk' disease phenotype. Identifying these children is clinically challenging, as overtreatment may expose them to unnecessary risks and costs, whereas undertreatment may allow irreversible bowel damage and complications to develop. This narrative review summarises the current evidence on the definition, assessment, treatment, and monitoring of low-risk paediatric CD, highlighting existing knowledge gaps and future research priorities. At present, no consensus definition of low-risk paediatric CD exists, and disease classification relies largely on the absence of recognised high-risk features rather than validated criteria. Similarly, unlike adult practice, no paediatric prognostic model is available to identify children likely to follow a persistently mild disease course. Current assessment requires integration of clinical indices, inflammatory biomarkers, endoscopy, cross-sectional imaging, and evaluation of growth and nutritional status. Dietary treatment (Exclusive Enteral Nutrition and emerging dietary strategies, including the CD Exclusion Diet [CDED] and the Tasty & Healthy [T&H]] remains the commonest induction therapy. Budesonide or antibiotics (azithromycin and metronidazole) represent an appropriate alternative for selected children. CDED and the T&H diet may also represent attractive medium term treatment options, although robust maintenance data are still awaited. Prospective studies are needed to establish a consensus definition, develop paediatric-specific prediction models, optimise risk stratification, and determine the most effective long-term therapeutic and monitoring approaches for the 'low-risk' population.

title: Treatment Response and Oncologic Outcomes Following Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy Switch in Localized Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background and objectives Many patients undergoing neoadjuvant therapy for localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) experience treatment intolerance or disease progression during initial therapy. Although chemotherapy switch is increasingly utilized, response rates and oncologic outcomes remain poorly defined. Methods Patients were identified from a prospectively maintained database of individuals undergoing neoadjuvant therapy for localized PDAC from 2012 to 2023. Eligible patients underwent chemotherapy switch between 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine regimens with curative intent. Favorable response was defined as complete or partial radiographic response by RECIST, or stable disease with a ≥ 50% decline in CA 19-9 relative to levels before switch. Outcomes were measured from the date of chemotherapy switch. Results Out of 161 patients, 41% achieved favorable response. Body/tail, borderline resectable, and locally advanced disease were independently associated with nonfavorable response. Among favorable responders, 49% underwent resection versus 11% of nonresponders. Favorable response was independently associated with improved progression-free and overall survival, including among unresected patients. Overall, 47% derived meaningful oncologic benefit through favorable response, resection, or both. Conclusions Chemotherapy switch offers a reasonable strategy in select patients with localized PDAC experiencing inadequate response or intolerance of initial therapy. This composite response framework identifies chemosensitive tumor biology, informs surgical decision-making, and stratifies prognosis.

title: CT-Based Radiomics for Preoperative Prediction of Surgical Margins in Pancreatic Head Cancer: A Tool for Selecting Patients for Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy.
abstract: Background Microscopic margin involvement (≤ 1 mm) strongly predicts poor prognosis in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Adjuvant chemotherapy (ACT) after upfront resection fails to fully mitigate this risk. It remains uncertain whether neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) can neutralize the adverse prognostic impact of impending ≤ 1 mm margins. Methods Prognostic significance of ≤ 1 mm margins was assessed in an upfront-resection cohort (n = 228) using multivariable Cox regression. A separate cohort (n = 110; 52 NACT, 58 upfront surgery) compared overall survival (OS) by margin status. A CT-based radiomics model using a Laplacian-Dirichlet operator was developed to predict ≤ 1 mm margins and externally validated (n = 230). Results ≤ 1 mm margins independently predicted worse OS vs. > 1 mm (15.0 vs. 24.0 months, p = 0.005). ACT numerically extended OS for ≤ 1 mm patients (16.0 vs. 15.0 months, p = 0.271) but did not close the survival gap. Notably, ≤ 1 mm patients receiving NACT achieved median OS of 29.4 months-comparable to > 1 mm upfront patients (31.6 months)-and significantly better than ≤ 1 mm upfront patients (19.6 months, p = 0.045). The model predicted ≤ 1 mm margins with AUCs of 0.772 (95% CI: 0.705-0.838) and 0.723 (95% CI: 0.657-0.789) in internal and external validation. Conclusion NACT-not ACT-selectively rescues high-risk patients destined for ≤ 1 mm margins. Our radiomics model enables preoperative identification, supporting personalized neoadjuvant therapy.

title: A Rat Tail Cyclic Compression Model for Studying Intervertebral Disc Mechanobiology.
abstract: Background Intervertebral disc (IVD) responses vary with loading magnitude, frequency, and duration. Existing loading systems are often mechanically complex and costly, while device input alone may not represent disc deformation. We developed a five-channel motor-driven system to relate graded cyclic displacement to mechanical and tissue responses. Methods Twenty 11-week-old male Sprague-Dawley rats were assigned to sham, low (0.4 mm), moderate (0.8 mm), and high (1.2 mm) compression groups ( n = 5 per group). Eight additional rats underwent characterization of peak compressive force, disc height deformation, wedge angulation, and sagittal plane anterior-posterior (A-P) translation. Outcomes included imaging, histology, cartilaginous endplate morphometry, and immunohistochemistry. Results Displacements of 0.4, 0.8, and 1.2 mm generated peak compressive forces of 3.94 ± 0.46, 8.69 ± 1.15, and 14.54 ± 1.31 N and radiographic disc height deformations of 13.00% ± 4.05%, 31.11% ± 8.38%, and 58.08% ± 10.27%, respectively. Wedge angle and sagittal plane A-P centroid offset did not differ significantly across the four displacement states ( p > 0.05). After 4 weeks of cyclic loading, the low compression group resembled the sham group. Moderate compression preserved disc structure and increased matrix marker positive areas. High compression caused disc narrowing, T2 signal loss, nucleus pulposus disruption, increased MMP-13 positive area, reduced cartilaginous endplate dimensions, and more frequent and severe endplate abnormalities. Conclusions Prescribed displacement produced graded mechanical and tissue responses, with axial disc height reduction as the predominant group level radiographic deformation. This simple, low-cost system provides an amplitude tunable platform for intervertebral disc mechanobiology research.

title: Development of a Multimodal Model Combining Imaging and Clinical Data to Predict Bone Cement Leakage During Vertebroplasty for Fresh Thoracolumbar Compression Fractures.
abstract: Background Bone cement leakage is a common complication of percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP), but perioperative risk stratification remains challenging. Existing models based on single-source clinical or imaging features have limited performance. This study aimed to develop and validate multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) models integrating clinical, imaging, and radiomics features to predict bone cement leakage during PVP. Methods This multicenter study included 486 treated vertebrae from 378 patients at the North, South, and Shenshan campuses of our hospital. The treated vertebra was the prediction unit, while all vertebrae from the same patient were retained in the same dataset partition and cross-validation fold. Clinical variables, conventional CT imaging features, and CT-based radiomics features were extracted. Logistic regression identified independent risk factors. Six machine-learning algorithms were used to construct clinical, imaging, radiomics, and multimodal models. Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, F1 score, and decision curve analysis. Independent external and prospective validations were performed, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used for model interpretation. Results Among the 486 treated vertebrae, 215 (44.2%) had cement leakage. Higher body mass index (BMI), greater cement injection volume, cortical destruction, and posterior wall involvement were independently associated with leakage. Multimodal models generally achieved higher AUCs than the corresponding single-modality models, with AUCs of 0.902-0.939 in the internal test cohort, 0.722-0.929 in the external validation cohort, and 0.834-0.925 in the prospective validation cohort. Patient-level aggregation and one-vertebra-per-patient sensitivity analyses yielded broadly comparable discrimination. SHAP identified cortical destruction, cement injection volume, and posterior wall involvement as the most influential predictors. Conclusions The multimodal models demonstrated good and generally consistent discrimination across the internal test, external validation, and prospective validation cohorts and may support perioperative risk assessment and individualized cement injection planning during PVP.

title: Super-Resolution Ultrasound for Lymph Node Evaluation: Diagnostic Value of Static Time-Point Parameters Versus Dynamic Temporal Changes.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate quantitative super-resolution ultrasound (SRUS) parameters (static central-to-peripheral ratios and dynamic temporal changes) for differentiating benign and metastatic lymph nodes, and to compare the performance of corresponding predictive models. Methods A prospective study included 172 pathologically confirmed lymph nodes (100 benign, 72 metastatic). SRUS was performed to derive density and velocity parameters, with central-to-peripheral ratios and temporal changes calculated. Static and dynamic models were constructed using univariate analysis, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), and logistic regression. Model performance was assessed by cross-validation, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration, decision curve analysis, and clinical impact curve. Results Metastatic lymph nodes showed significantly lower central-to-peripheral ratios of density and velocity parameters but higher relative temporal changes in density SD and velocity SD compared with benign nodes (all P < .05). The static time-point model retained 2 SRUS variables (Mean.Density_C_P_T2, Max.Density_C_P_T3), yielding a full-sample AUC of 0.8607. The temporal change model included 2 dynamic parameters (Velocity SD change from T1 to T2, Mean density change from T2 to T3) and achieved a higher AUC of 0.8715, with better accuracy, specificity, and model fit. Both models showed favorable calibration and clinical net benefit. Conclusion Quantitative SRUS parameters effectively reflect pathological angiogenesis in metastatic lymph nodes. The temporal change model provides superior diagnostic performance over the static time-point model and may serve as a reliable noninvasive tool for distinguishing benign from metastatic lymph nodes.

A prospective study included 172 pathologically confirmed lymph nodes (100 benign, 72 metastatic). SRUS was performed to derive density and velocity parameters, with central-to-peripheral ratios and temporal changes calculated. Static and dynamic models were constructed using univariate analysis, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), and logistic regression. Model performance was assessed by cross-validation, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration, decision curve analysis, and clinical impact curve.

Results

Metastatic lymph nodes showed significantly lower central-to-peripheral ratios of density and velocity parameters but higher relative temporal changes in density SD and velocity SD compared with benign nodes (all P < .05). The static time-point model retained 2 SRUS variables (Mean.Density_C_P_T2, Max.Density_C_P_T3), yielding a full-sample AUC of 0.8607. The temporal change model included 2 dynamic parameters (Velocity SD change from T1 to T2, Mean density change from T2 to T3) and achieved a higher AUC of 0.8715, with better accuracy, specificity, and model fit. Both models showed favorable calibration and clinical net benefit.

Conclusion

Quantitative SRUS parameters effectively reflect pathological angiogenesis in metastatic lymph nodes. The temporal change model provides superior diagnostic performance over the static time-point model and may serve as a reliable noninvasive tool for distinguishing benign from metastatic lymph nodes.

title: Prenatal Ultrasound in Predicting the Need for Postnatal Surgery in Fetal Non-duodenal Small Bowel Dilation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: The accuracy of prenatal ultrasound in recognizing fetal non-duodenal small bowel dilation (ND-SBD) due to obstructive conditions requiring neonatal surgery is not well established. We assessed the positive predictive value (PPV) of prenatal 2-dimensional (2D) ultrasound measurement of the small bowel diameter for identifying fetuses with ND-SBD who will require postnatal surgical intervention. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane with terms related to fetal bowel dilation and postnatal outcome. For each included study, we estimated the PPV of prenatal ultrasound in predicting the need for neonatal surgery among live-born, evaluable newborns classified as having a prenatal diagnosis of ND-SBD, and performed a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of proportions to estimate the pooled PPV across studies. We identified 10 manuscripts, comprising 390 fetuses with a prenatal diagnosis of ND-SBD, of which 341 from 9 studies had data available for analysis. The observed PPV for postnatal surgery ranged from 8 to 82%, with a pooled estimate of 56% (90% credible interval (CrI) [44%, 67%]). Heterogeneity between studies was elevated, with an I 2 of 84.8% (90% CrI [68.3%, 92.4%]) and a wide 90% posterior predictive interval of 19-89%, indicating substantial variability in the PPV across populations. Most studies presented high or unclear risk of bias and applicability concerns based on QUADAS-2 evaluation. 2D prenatal ultrasound evaluation of the fetal small intestine diameter has a moderate ability in predicting the need for postnatal surgery due to ND-SBD conditions. The substantial between-study heterogeneity and wide posterior predictive interval indicate considerable variation in the predictive value across populations and clinical settings, limiting the interpretation of the pooled PPV alone. Our findings highlight the need for prospective studies to better define the normal development of the fetal small intestine and identify prenatal ultrasound markers predicting non-duodenal small bowel abnormalities.

title: Predictive Model for Early Identification of Poor Prognosis in Kidney Transplant Recipients Based on Ultrasound Hemodynamic Parameters Combined with Clinical and Laboratory Indicators: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Objectives This study aimed to identify kidney transplant recipients with functioning grafts at the 3-month post-transplant who were at high risk of subsequent adverse graft outcomes. We developed predictive models and nomograms integrating ultrasound hemodynamic, clinical, and laboratory parameters. Methods We analyzed 376 kidney transplant recipients enrolled from January 2020 to April 2023. The 2020-2022 cohort was randomly divided into a training set (n = 200) and an internal random holdout set (validation set 1; n = 131). The subsequently enrolled 2023 cohort was retained as the temporal validation set (validation set 2; n = 45). All ultrasound predictors were assessed at the approximately 3-month post-transplant. Risk factors were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) and logistic regression. Predictive models were constructed using logistic regression and 5 machine-learning algorithms. Model performance was evaluated in terms of discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility, and a nomogram was developed for visualization. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to interpret the machine-learning models. Results The final logistic regression model included graft renal segmental artery resistance index (Grsa RI), preoperative albumin, and postoperative day 5 platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (Po5 PLR). Its AUCs were 0.893 in the internal random holdout set (validation set 1) and 0.859 in the temporal validation set (validation set 2). The random forest model, selected on the basis of the highest training-set AUC among the machine-learning models, achieved AUCs of 0.916 and 0.821 in validation sets 1 and 2, respectively. DeLong tests showed no statistically significant difference in AUC between the logistic regression and random forest models in either validation cohort (p = .958 and p = .561, respectively). Preoperative albumin, Po5 PLR, and Grsa RI were independently associated with adverse graft outcomes. Conclusions The prediction models effectively identified high-risk recipients using pre- and postoperative variables, providing an actionable strategy for early intervention to improve transplant outcomes by targeting modifiable factors.

title: Individualised total knee arthroplasty results in low reintervention rates for stiffness and instability in 1000 consecutive knees, regardless of intraoperative bone recuts or polyethylene thickness.
abstract: Purpose Individualised total knee arthroplasty (TKA) aims to restore the pre-arthritic anatomy, but concerns persist regarding ligament imbalance, as only two polyethylene insert thicknesses are available. This study aimed to evaluate revision and reintervention rates, especially for stiffness and instability, after individualised TKA, and whether intraoperative adjustments influenced these outcomes. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 1000 consecutive primary TKAs implanted using a CT-based individualised system with a 1-year minimum follow-up. The primary endpoint was any revision TKA. Secondary analyses evaluated reintervention for stiffness or instability and the association between reinterventions and (1) bone recuts and (2) polyethylene thickness. Survival was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method. Results At a mean follow-up of 4.2 ± 1.8 years, 12 revision TKA (1.2%) and 29 reinterventions (2.9%) were recorded. All procedures were completed as planned with only two polyethylene insert thicknesses. Revision-free survival was 99.4% (95% confidence interval [CI] 98.7-99.7) at 1 year and 98.7% (95% CI 97.7-99.3) at 5 years. Reoperation-free survival was 98.1% (95% CI 97.0-98.8) and 97.0% (95% CI 95.7-97.9) at 1 and 5 years, respectively. Stiffness-related procedures occurred in nine cases (0.9%), and instability-related revision was observed in one case (0.1%). Bone recuts were performed in 42.8% of knees. No significant association was found between revision risk and bone recuts or polyethylene thickness. Conclusion In this large consecutive cohort, individualised TKA was associated with low rates of revision and of reintervention for stiffness and instability. Intraoperative adjustments (bone recuts, polyethylene thickness changes) were not associated with a higher revision rate. Level of evidence Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Gracilis tendon harvest for ACL reconstruction impairs gracilis muscle volume recovery and may adversely affect adjacent thigh musculature. MRI-based outcomes from a subgroup of patients enroled in the DOSTAR randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Purpose Segmentation of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows accurate calculation of muscle volumes. The Dual Or Single Tendon Anterior cruciate ligament Reconstruction (DOSTAR) study is a prospective randomized controlled trial investigating a semitendinosus (ST) graft with adjustable button tibial fixation versus a dual tendon semitendinosus and gracilis (STG) graft with screw tibial fixation in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). The purpose of the present study is to investigate differences in thigh muscle volume at 6 and 12 months between these treatment groups. Methods Patients were randomized and underwent ACLR using either a ST or STG graft construct. MRI of bilateral thighs was completed at 6 and 12 months post-operatively. Muscle volumes were measured in both thighs at both time points in both groups. Results A total of 38 patients underwent MRI scanning at 6 and 12 months. There was a significant difference in the interval volume change of gracilis in the STG group compared to the ST group (-1.6 cm 3 ± 4.6 vs. +2.8 cm 3 ± 6.8, p = 0.026). Interval gracilis hypertrophy occurred in 35% (7/20) of cases in the STG group and 67% of cases (12/18) in the ST group (p = 0.103). Adductor longus (AddL) also demonstrated a significant difference in interval volume change between the STG and ST group (-2.4 cm 3 ± 12.0 vs. +11.1 cm 3 ± 21.2, p = 0.020). AddL hypertrophy occurred in 30% of cases (6/20) in the STG group and 72% (13/18) in the ST group (p = 0.022). All other muscles had no significant differences noted in muscle recovery between groups. Linear regression analysis demonstrated a significant positive relationship between interval changes in gracilis and AddL volumes (p < 0.001). Conclusions The present study provides MRI evidence that gracilis tendon harvest was associated with persistent impairment of gracilis muscle recovery and may also adversely affect AddL. This adds to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of ST with adjustable button graft constructs for hamstring ACLR. Level of evidence Level II, subgroup analysis of prospective, double-blinded, randomized controlled trial.

title: Meniscus centralization: Are we treating meniscal extrusion as the cause of osteoarthritis or simply its consequence?
abstract: Residual meniscal extrusion (ME) is considered an important factor jeopardizing the long-term success of otherwise technically successful medial meniscus posterior root (MMPR) repair. Biomechanical and clinical studies have shown that meniscal centralization can reduce extrusion, restore contact mechanics and improve short-term clinical outcomes. However, an important paradox remains: many patients with pre-existing osteoarthritis (OA) and persistent ME after MMPR repair maintain good clinical outcomes despite continued radiographic progression. Although the biomechanical rationale for centralization is compelling, its clinical value may be more complex in the middle-aged, degenerative knee. Progressive changes in tissue elasticity, capsular attenuation and joint biology may contribute to meniscal displacement, suggesting that ME may be less a primary driver of degeneration than a manifestation of an underlying OA. This raises a fundamental question: Are we treating the right target? Is residual ME a modifiable driver of disease progression, or does it primarily reflect the natural history of joint degeneration? This Editorial critically examines the emerging evidence on meniscal centralization, explores the clinical relevance of residual ME and highlights key questions that can guide future research.

title: Bone marrow stimulation improves 12-month clinical outcomes after isolated meniscal repair: A double-blind randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Purpose To compare short-term clinical outcomes and meniscal healing on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 12 months between standard arthroscopic meniscal repair and repair augmented with bone marrow stimulation (BMS) in isolated meniscal tears. Methods In this prospective, two-centre, double-blind randomized controlled trial, patients aged 18-60 years with an isolated meniscal tear confirmed on MRI were randomized 1:1 to standard repair or repair augmented with BMS. Medial, lateral and bicompartmental tears were included. The primary outcome was the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective score at 12 months. Secondary outcomes were the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), Lysholm score, Tegner activity scale, pain on a visual analogue scale (VAS), patient satisfaction, operative time, adverse events and meniscal healing on 12-month MRI (3.0-T) (Crues classification, two-blinded assessors). Results Fifty patients (mean age 40.2 years; 21 male and 29 female) were randomized; all completed follow-up. Baseline characteristics were balanced; the augmented group received significantly more sutures (4.2 ± 1.4 vs. 3.3 ± 1.1; p = 0.011) and had fewer horizontal tears (44% vs. 76%; p = 0.042). At 6 months, Lysholm and satisfaction scores already favoured the augmented group. At 12 months, it was superior for the IKDC score (82.5 ± 12.6 vs. 56.5 ± 18.5), WOMAC score (14.6 ± 20.0 vs. 41.8 ± 32.5), Lysholm score (91.8 ± 6.4 vs. 72.6 ± 17.2), Tegner activity scale (median 5.0, interquartile range [IQR] 4.0-6.0 vs. 3.0, IQR 2.0-4.0), pain (0.6 ± 0.7 vs. 2.3 ± 2.3) and satisfaction (9.7 ± 0.6 vs. 7.9 ± 1.7); all p < 0.05. MRI healing did not differ between groups (p = 0.783; unhealed: 2/25 [8%] per group); operative time was similar, and no complications occurred within 12 months. Conclusions In this cohort, BMS augmentation was associated with superior patient-reported outcomes at 12 months, without additional complications or an increase in operative time. Meniscal healing on MRI did not differ between groups. These positive short-term findings helped to prove the benefit of BMS augmentation, although confirmation in larger trials with longer follow-up and structural assessment is required to clarify the effectiveness, durability and indications of BMS. Level of evidence Level I, therapeutic randomized controlled trial.

title: Bone-patellar tendon-bone and quadriceps tendon autografts are associated with a higher 1-year risk of thigh muscle injury after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in competitive male athletes: A retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Purpose To investigate the association between anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) graft type and subsequent thigh muscle injury in athletes involved in pivoting sports. Methods A retrospective observational study was conducted on 221 ACLRs performed in 199 competitive male athletes involved in pivoting sports, classified according to graft donor site: extensor mechanism (bone-patellar tendon-bone [BPTB] or quadriceps tendon) and flexor mechanism (hamstring tendon). Only athletes who returned to sport and completed a minimum of 12 months of follow-up were included. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-confirmed thigh muscle injuries occurring within the first year following the discharge date were identified and classified by muscle group injured and graft type. Results Thirty-five athletes (15.8%) sustained at least one MRI-confirmed thigh muscle injury (41 muscle-group-level injuries in total) in the year after discharge from ACLR. Athletes who received a graft from the extensor mechanism had a higher proportion of any thigh muscle injury than those with hamstring grafts (27/133, 20.3% vs. 8/88, 9.1%; absolute risk difference 11.2%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.4-20.0; odds ratio [OR] 2.45, 95% CI 1.12-5.88; p = 0.037). Muscle-group analyses showed no significant differences for hamstring injury or quadriceps injury. All six adductor injuries occurred in the extensor donor group (4.5% vs. 0%), but this difference was not statistically robust. After adjustment, none of the three muscle-group comparisons remained significant. Conclusion Extensor mechanism grafts were associated with a higher proportion of athletes sustaining any thigh muscle injury in the year following discharge from rehabilitation; although absolute rates were low, no individual muscle group showed a significant difference. Level of evidence Level III retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Elective Neck Dissection in cT1-4 N0M0 Submandibular Gland Cancer.
abstract: Objective To investigate occult nodal metastasis (ONM) and overall survival (OS) in patients undergoing elective neck dissection (END) for clinically node-negative submandibular gland cancer (SMGC). Methods The 2006 to 2018 National Cancer Database was retrospectively reviewed for patients with cT1-4 N0M0 SMGC undergoing surgical resection. Linear, binary logistic, Kaplan-Meier, and Cox proportional hazards regression models were implemented. Results A high proportion of patients were female (N = 710, 54.6%) and White (N = 1059, 82.5%) with adenoid cystic carcinoma histology (N = 567, 43.6%) classified as cT1 (N = 545, 41.9%). A minority of patients (N = 255, 19.6%) underwent END. Academic/research reporting facility, high grade, cT3, and cT4 classification were associated with higher odds of undergoing END; Medicare insurance was associated with lower odds (p < 0.05). ONM was identified in 63 (24.7%) patients undergoing END. The rate of ONM increased with cT classification (13.2% in cT1, 27.9% in cT2, 22.0% in cT3, and 50.0% in cT4) and grade (6.5% in well-differentiated, 9.5% in moderately differentiated, and 40.3% in poorly differentiated). END was not associated with OS (hazard ratio [HR] 1.11, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.84-1.46, p = 0.461). However, ONM was associated with worse OS (HR 3.69, 95% CI, 2.25-6.05, p < 0.001); 5-year OS for patients without and with ONM was 83% and 50%, respectively (p < 0.001). Conclusion END is performed frequently in SMGC but is not associated with OS. Although the rate of ONM approaches 25%, these findings suggest that END should not be routinely performed for prognostic purposes alone, especially in the absence of adverse features. Level of evidence: 4

title: Impact of Corridor Morphology on Internal Auditory Canal Exposure in the Retrolabyrinthine Approach.
abstract: Objectives The retrolabyrinthine approach is a presigmoid, potentially hearing-preserving option for internal auditory canal (IAC) lesions, though exposure is limited by a narrow corridor. Endoscopic assistance may improve lateral visualization. This study compared projected radiographic versus postdissection IAC exposure using simulated 0° and 30° endoscopy and evaluated anatomic predictors of exposure. Methods Thirteen cadaver temporal bones underwent high-resolution computed tomography before and after IAC dissection with posterior semicircular canal preservation. The retrolabyrinthine approach was simulated using 3D segmentation in 0° and 30° endoscopic views. Total and accessible IAC volumes and the percentage of IAC accessible were compared between projected and postdissection models. Projections were compared with observed volumes using Wilcoxon signed-rank testing. Associations between anatomic covariates (corridor width, angle of approach, surgical freedom) and exposure were evaluated using Theil-Sen regression. Results Median IAC volume was 230.1 mm 3 (range 148.1-446.9). Surgical freedom ranged from 123.3-319.2 mm 2 (median 182.9), and angle of approach from 13.9° to 27.1° (median 19.9°). Projected exposures were 59.2% at 0° and 92.2% at 30°, versus 65.1% and 75.6% postdissection. Projection underestimated 0° exposure (-5.9%, p = 0.01) and overestimated 30° exposure (+16.7%, p = 0.048). Thirty-degree endoscopy improved exposure (p < 0.001). Each 1 mm increase in corridor width increased accessible volume by 8.46 mm 3 (0°) and 5.31 mm 3 (30°), and each 1° increase in angle of approach increased accessible volume by 4.98 mm 3 (0°) and 5.11 mm 3 (30°) (all p ≤ 0.04). Conclusions Endoscopic assistance improves exposure, although projections overestimate 30° exposure. Corridor width and angle of approach may inform preoperative selection. Level of evidence N/A.

title: External vs. Powered Endoscopic Dacryocystorhinostomy With Mitomycin C: A Randomized Study.
abstract: Objective(s) To compare the 12-month anatomical and functional outcomes of external dacryocystorhinostomy (ExDCR) and powered endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy (EnDCR) with intraoperative mitomycin C (MMC) in patients with primary acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction (PANDO). Methods This prospective, randomized, single-center clinical trial assessed 133 patients with PANDO for eligibility. Eligible participants were randomized 1:1 to ExDCR or powered EnDCR. Anatomical success was defined as ostium patency confirmed by nasal endoscopy and lacrimal irrigation, whereas functional success was defined as a Munk score ≤ 1 at 12 months. Results Anatomical success was achieved in 90% of patients after ExDCR and 100% after powered EnDCR, corresponding to an absolute between-group difference of 10 percentage points (95% CI, -3% to 26%; p = 0.237). Functional success was achieved in 87% and 97%, respectively, corresponding to an absolute between-group difference of 10 percentage points (95% CI, -6% to 27%; p = 0.353). Complete resolution of epiphora occurred in 80% and 93%, respectively (p = 0.254). Postoperative complications were predominantly mild and local. Conclusion Both ExDCR and powered EnDCR with intraoperative MMC achieved high anatomical and functional success rates at 12 months. Powered EnDCR showed numerically higher success rates, although the between-group differences were not statistically significant. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07754058 LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 2.

title: AI-Assisted Ni Classification in Nasopharyngeal NBI: Multicenter Validation and Reader Study.
abstract: Objective(s) To develop and validate an artificial intelligence (AI) system for standardized Ni classification of nasopharyngeal narrow-band imaging (NBI) and to evaluate whether AI assistance improves physician diagnostic consistency and biopsy-related decision making in a reader-study setting. Methods In this multicenter diagnostic study, 5404 high-quality nasopharyngeal NBI images were retrospectively collected. Lesion segmentation and five-class Ni classification networks were trained independently. Performance was evaluated in an internal test set, two independent external cohorts, and a recorded-video validation set. A prospective randomized multi-reader crossover study involving 12 physicians and 200 images from CHSZCAMS assessed the effect of AI assistance on diagnostic performance, inter-observer agreement, and potentially unnecessary biopsy decisions. Results In the two external cohorts, the model achieved accuracies of 0.889 and 0.873, with AUCs of 0.976 and 0.967, respectively. In recorded-video validation, accuracy was 0.888 and AUC was 0.974. AI assistance improved Fleiss kappa from 0.610 to 0.788 in junior physicians and from 0.744 to 0.870 in senior physicians (both p < 0.05). Potentially unnecessary biopsy decisions decreased from 21.6% to 10.3% in junior physicians and from 13.7% to 8.0% in senior physicians. Conclusion AI-assisted Ni classification showed consistent diagnostic performance across validation cohorts and improved physician agreement across experience levels. In this reader-study setting, AI assistance reduced potentially unnecessary biopsy decisions, supporting further evaluation as a second-reader tool for nasopharyngeal NBI interpretation. Level of evidence: 3

title: Regional Mitochondrial Density Maps Selective Posterior Atrophy in Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Background Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in the pathobiology of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the spatial relationship between regional energetic demand and patterns of neurodegeneration remains poorly understood, limiting mechanistic insight and development of disease-modifying therapies. Objectives This study tested whether regional mitochondrial density aligns with patterns of brain atrophy in PD, how this alignment differs across genetic groups, and whether the mitochondrial-atrophy axis associates with motor and cognitive features. Methods Structural magnetic resonance imaging data were analyzed from 849 individuals (210 healthy controls, 639 patients with PD). Principal component analysis (PCA) identified dominant atrophy axes and tested their association with regional mitochondrial density and complex I activity. Transcriptomic validation used Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression data restricted to 924 MitoCarta-annotated genes across 31 cortical regions. Results Participants with PD exhibited higher volumetric loss in limbic and subcortical regions than controls. PCA showed a posterior cortical axis of atrophy (PC3) that correlated positively with regional mitochondrial density and was more strongly expressed in LRRK2-PD than in sporadic PD. This axis was selectively associated with visuospatial dysfunction. Transcriptomic validation confirmed that regions of greater atrophy preferentially expressed mitochondrial genes, with mitoribosome assembly, mitochondrial DNA maintenance, and coenzyme Q biosynthesis emerging as the strongest pathway-level predictors. Conclusion These findings link the brain's regional mitochondrial landscape to spatially patterned neurodegeneration in PD, with amplification in LRRK2 mutation carriers. This mitochondrial atrophy axis may provide a biologically informed marker aiding patient stratification and mitochondrial-targeted therapeutic development. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Anatomically Tailored Partial Hallux Transfer for an Oblique Fingertip Amputation.
abstract: Partial toe transfer enables reconstruction of complex fingertip defects involving the nail unit, distal phalanx, and pulp. We report an oblique middle-fingertip amputation with extensive loss of the distal phalanx, reconstructed with a highly distal unilateral partial hallux transfer. Selective harvesting of a unilateral hallux tuft segment and a small adjacent portion of the plantar shaft enabled anatomical reconstruction of the recipient osseous defect. At 30 months, the reconstructed fingertip maintained satisfactory contour, nail-bed morphology, and nail growth. Radiographs showed excellent anatomical correspondence between the transferred bone and the recipient distal phalanx, particularly in the volar tuft and shaft contours, with no apparent bone resorption. Joint motion was preserved, static two-point discrimination was 3 mm, and the QuickDASH score was 9.1. The donor germinal matrix and most of the distal phalanx were preserved, allowing conservative donor-site management without additional flap reconstruction. The patient returned to farm work without functional limitations attributable to either the reconstructed finger or the donor toe. A focused review of 10 studies revealed a trend toward increasingly selective partial toe transfers, but detailed anatomical documentation of bone harvesting for oblique fingertip defects remained limited. This case suggests that anatomically tailored bone harvesting may extend the application of selective partial hallux transfer to oblique fingertip amputations while minimizing donor-site morbidity.

title: Reliability-weighted patch learning for synthetic CT reconstruction in head and neck adaptive radiotherapy: A proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Background Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is essential for adaptive radiotherapy (ART) but is limited by poor image quality. Existing deep learning methods for synthetic CT (sCT) generation face a critical trade-off: diffusion models offer high fidelity but are impractically slow, while fast-inference networks often lack structural accuracy and optimization stability. Purpose To develop HQ-PatchNet, a reliability-driven deep learning framework designed to improve CBCT-to-sCT image quality while maintaining rapid inference speed for online ART workflows. Methods HQ-PatchNet utilizes a vision transformer (ViT)-integrated CycleGAN architecture. It introduces a reliability-driven, SSIM-based selective patch weighting mechanism controlled by a temperature decay schedule. This dynamically suppresses artifact-dominated regions and focuses optimization on anatomically reliable structures. The model was evaluated on 304 paired head-and-neck (HN) scans against conventional networks and recent diffusion models using quantitative metrics (MAE, SSIM, NCC, PSNR), computational speed, and clinical dosimetric accuracy (3D gamma index, 2%/2 mm). Results HQ-PatchNet improved image quality, reducing Mean Absolute Error (MAE) from 44.81 ± 11.24 HU to 11.85 ± 4.31 HU and achieving an SSIM of 0.960 ± 0.055, comparable to state-of-the-art diffusion models. Inference required only 6.42 ± 1.71 s per volume, compared to > 15 min for diffusion approaches. The model reduced severe metal and truncation artifacts, and representative qualitative assessment suggested visually consistent sCT generation under interfractional anatomical variation. Dosimetric assessment of complex HN IMRT plans yielded a high average gamma passing rate of 99.32 ± 0.56%. Conclusions HQ-PatchNet provides a computationally efficient and clinically promising approach for daily CBCT-guided online ART by improving CBCT-to-sCT image quality while maintaining rapid inference speed. Further contour-based, multi-institutional, and multi-site validation remains necessary to confirm its broader clinical utility.

title: Learning global and local representations for generalized category discovery in neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved notable success in closed-set classification of neurodegenerative diseases, but its performance degrades significantly in more realistic open-set settings, such as discovering rare or novel disease subtypes from unlabeled data that are not seen during training. This study introduces, to our knowledge, the first framework for generalized category discovery (GCD) in neurodegenerative diseases using MRI. It aims to leverage labeled data from known categories to automatically identify novel categories within unlabeled datasets. We propose a GCD framework integrating semi-supervised contrastive learning with global-local representation learning to jointly optimize feature learning. Globally, we enforce consistency between weakly augmented views of the same instance by aligning their similarity relationships with other embeddings in a support queue. Locally, we treat neighborhood embeddings from the support queue as positive pairs for cross-instance contrastive learning, enhancing fine-grained discrimination. This dual strategy results in a unified learning objective that is applicable to both labeled and unlabeled data, effectively narrowing the representation gap among semantically similar instances. We evaluate our method on a benchmark dataset comprising six neurodegenerative diseases, with over 1500 patient samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms representative state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our method achieves 66.02% Accuracy and 60.59% Normalized Mutual Information on all categories, and 54.53% Accuracy and 16.67% Normalized Mutual Information on novel categories, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Our framework underscores the model's robustness and its practical value in discovering new neurodegenerative disease conditions, highlighting its potential for advancing open-set diagnostic AI.

title: A novel image-domain denoising method for triple-material decomposition in dual-energy CT.
abstract: Background Triple-material decomposition (TMD) holds significant clinical value in dual-energy computed tomography (DECT), as it enables simultaneous differentiation of bone, soft tissue, and contrast agents-three key components commonly targeted in clinical imaging assessments. However, the inherent noise amplification artifact associated with material decomposition remains a critical technical bottleneck that restricts its widespread clinical translation. Purpose To address this limitation, this study proposes an image-domain denoising strategy to mitigate noise amplification, thereby improving the quantitative accuracy and qualitative quality of TMD in DECT. Method First, DECT images were transformed into amplitude and argument components via vectorization. Second, a spectral joint bilateral filtering algorithm was developed to specifically denoise the argument images, leveraging inter-spectral correlation to preserve structural details while suppressing noise. Subsequently, denoised DECT images were reconstructed using the original amplitude and denoised argument components. TMD was performed with soft tissue, bone, and contrast agent as basis materials, utilizing two decomposition approaches: direct matrix inversion (DMI) and the penalized weighted least squares-expectation maximization-loop (PWLS-EP-LOOP) iterative method. The proposed denoising strategy was validated on a benchtop micro-CT system, with evaluations conducted on both a customized anthropomorphic phantom and an in vivo mouse model injected with ExiTron nano 6000 contrast agent. Results For DMI-based decomposition, the proposed method achieved noise reduction rates (NRRs) of 68.9% in soft tissue images, 74.4% in contrast-enhanced images, and 78.7% in bone images. For PWLS-EP-LOOP-based iterative decomposition, the corresponding NRRs were 22.4% (soft tissue), 48.6% (contrast agent), and 37.5% (bone). Furthermore, the number of iteration cycles required for convergence in the PWLS-EP-LOOP algorithm was reduced by 75.4%, substantially improving computational efficiency. Conclusion Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed image-domain denoising method, tailored for DECT TMD, effectively suppresses noise in both DMI and iterative workflows while preserving structural fidelity. This work thus provides a promising solution to enhance the clinical utility of DECT material decomposition.

title: Bias-corrected respiratory motion standard deviation from amplitude-binned 4D-MRI for radiotherapy planning.
abstract: Background Respiratory-resolved magnetic resonance imaging (4D-MRI) provides superior soft-tissue contrast for characterizing respiratory motion in radiotherapy, but its geometric fidelity depends on the reconstruction and binning strategy. As with 4D-CT, peak-to-peak amplitude derived from binned 4D-MRI is prone to underestimation. However, as acquisitions span many respiratory cycles, the standard deviation (SD) of motion, required for probability-based planning approaches such as mid-ventilation, may be estimated accurately, provided binning-induced bias is corrected. Purpose To develop and validate a motion SD estimator for equal-probability amplitude-binned 4D-MRI data that corrects for systematic underestimation caused by intra-bin motion variability. Methods 4D-MRI data were acquired on a dynamic motion phantom driven by five patient-derived respiratory traces. Images were reconstructed using both a standard non-uniform fast Fourier transform (NUFFT) and the compressed sensing-based XD-GRASP algorithm with varying numbers (2-20) of equal-probability respiratory amplitude bins. An SD estimator based on the law of total variance was implemented to correct for intra-bin variance. The accuracy of peak-to-peak amplitude and SD was evaluated against ground-truth physical phantom motion, with performance under deformable motion tested on a digital phantom (CoMBAT). Results Both reconstruction methods underestimated true peak-to-peak motion. While the inter-bin SD calculation also underestimated motion variability, the proposed correction substantially mitigated this bias. It yielded robust SD estimates with median residual underestimation of 0.13 mm (5 bins) and 0.11 mm (10 bins) across patient traces. In CoMBAT, the absolute bias of the total SD estimate was below 3% from five bins onward. Conclusions The proposed estimator provides an accurate measurement of respiratory motion SD from amplitude-binned 4D-MRI by accounting for intra-bin variability. This supports the reliability of 4D-MRI for planning strategies dependent on motion probability distributions. Additionally, the confirmed underestimation of peak-to-peak amplitude highlights a fundamental limitation in defining internal target volumes directly from binned 4D-MRI.

title: Impact of correlated PBPK parameters on intra-patient global sensitivity analysis in molecular radiotherapy.
abstract: Background Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models integrated into digital twins provide a robust framework for optimizing individualized molecular radiotherapy (MRT). Nevertheless, uncertainties in PBPK-model-derived dosimetry can compromise the reliability of dosimetry-guided treatment planning and individualized therapy decisions. Purpose This study employs intra-patient global sensitivity analysis (GSA) to assess the influence of uncertainty and correlations among PBPK model parameters on estimated kidney and tumor absorbed doses (ADs) in prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted theragnostics. Methods Data from 10 patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who underwent pre-therapeutic [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-I&T PET/CT and a cycle of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-I&T therapy, followed by post-therapeutic SPECT/CT scans at Days 1 and 4 post-injection, were analyzed. A previously established whole-body PBPK model for PSMA-targeted radionuclide therapy was used as the baseline model. Fifteen model parameters, their standard errors, and inter-parameter correlations were estimated by fitting to measured time-activity data and subsequently evaluated using intra-patient GSA based on the Kucherenko method implemented in UQLab. In one approach, correlations were ignored to identify the direct influences of uncertainty in input parameters on ADs. In a second approach, correlations were included to reflect realistic parameter distributions and to capture indirect effects arising from parameter interdependencies. Pharmacokinetics were simulated to estimate therapeutic kidney and tumor ADs as well as main- and total-effect indices ( Si,SiT) . Sensitivity indices, ADs, and their associated uncertainty metrics were compared between scenarios with and without parameter correlations. Results Including parameter correlations in the GSA yielded kidney ADs of 4.2 Gy [3.0-7.2 Gy] (median [min-max]) with standard deviations (SDs) of 0.5 Gy [0.4-0.9 Gy] and tumor ADs of 10.1 Gy [2.0-26.8 Gy] with SDs of 1.7 Gy [0.6-3.4 Gy]. Neglecting correlations resulted in significantly higher uncertainties in ADs, by a factor of 1.2 [1.0-1.8] for both kidneys and tumors. Kidney ADs were most sensitive to kidney receptor density ( Si=0.3[0.1-0.6], SiT=0.7[0.6-0.8] ) and to the filtered fraction of renal blood flow (Si=0.2[0.1-0.3], SiT=0.3[0.1-0.4]) . Tumor ADs were most affected by tumor receptor density ( Si=0.7[0.1-1.0], SiT=0.8[0.3-1.0] ). The involvement of parameter correlations did not alter the identification of the parameters most influential on AD estimates and further reduced computational runtime. Conclusions Incorporating parameter correlations into intra-patient GSA reduced the estimated uncertainty associated with ADs, underscoring the importance of preserving parameter dependencies when propagating uncertainty in PBPK-based individualized MRT. The identification of key PBPK parameters governing kidney and tumor ADs remained stable when including correlation, confirming the robustness of the underlying model structure.

title: An anatomy-aware spatio-temporal generative extrapolation network for distal ascending aorta restoration in standard echocardiographic views.
abstract: Background In two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), the standard parasternal long-axis (PLAX) view enables reliable evaluation of the aortic valve and aortic root. Owing to the limited field of view of the ultrasound probe and rib-window occlusion, the distal ascending aorta (AA) is frequently truncated, compromising the diagnosis of aortic aneurysm and dilation. Purpose We aim to address the incomplete visualization of the distal AA in standard PLAX views. By aggregating fragmented anatomical features intermittently visible in adjacent frames, we enhance the clarity of vessel wall edges and generate the distal AA structure, thereby completing the missing AA imagery in standard PLAX views. Materials and methods We retrospectively collected 1160 TTE videos from Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital (August 2022 - December 2024), all showing complete AA anatomy. After de-identification, 1059 cases were randomly split into training/validation/test sets (6:2:2), and 101 cases were reserved for observer agreement experiments. An additional 152 videos from three different device models (EPIQ CVX, GE Voluson E10, Resona A20T) formed an external validation set. Two training data types were constructed: (i) dual-view synchronous data - a standard PLAX sequence and an AO-PLAX sequence acquired after a cranial probe shift, phase-matched at end diastole (ED); and (ii) locally masked data - the distal AA region was masked, forcing the model to infer missing anatomy from left-side context. Input sequences of five frames (ED ± 2) were extracted. The proposed Spatio-Temporal Ascending-Aorta generative adversarial network (STAA-GAN) first aligns adjacent frames using an Edge Boosted Feature Alignment (EBFA) module with multi-stage modulated deformable convolutions. A channel-wise fusion strategy then aggregates temporally aligned features. The fused representation is fed into a Swin-UNet generator enhanced with a Strip based Cross window Prediction (SCP) module to capture long-range structural dependencies. Training employs a composite loss including pixel reconstruction, feature reconstruction, texture consistency, relativistic average least-squares GAN (RaLSGAN), temporal coherence, and structure-aware terms, with data-dependent weighting. Statistical analyzes included Bland-Altman, Passing-Bablok regression, paired t-tests with Cohen's d, Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, and two one-sided tests (TOST, Δ=0.2cm ). Results STAA-GAN achieved the best image-quality values among the compared methods, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) = 22.51 dB, structural similarity index (SSIM) = 0.7574, multi-scale structural similarity index (MS-SSIM) = 0.8598, and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) = 0.1758. All 12 pairwise comparisons (SRN, IOH, and U-Transformer versus STAA-GAN, designated as the reference group) remained statistically significant after Bonferroni correction ( α1=0.00417 ), with absolute effect sizes ranging from 0.255 to 3.439. The per-frame inference time was 203 ms. In clinical consistency validation, the mean difference between measurements on generated and original images was ≤0.01 cm with 95% limits of agreement within ±0.13 cm; TOST with Δ=0.2 cm confirmed clinical equivalence for all comparisons ( p<0.001 ). The segmentation Dice coefficient on generated images averaged 0.913±0.045 across five cross-validation folds. External validation on three different ultrasound devices (Philips, GE, Mindray) maintained consistent equivalence (TOST p<0.001 , Cohen's d<0.2 ). These results demonstrate that STAA-GAN produces clinically interchangeable distal ascending aorta images with high fidelity and real-time feasibility. Conclusions STAA-GAN enables extrapolation of the missing distal ascending aorta in standard PLAX views, achieving improved image quality and clinically equivalent diameter measurements on both internal and external validation datasets. These findings support its potential for assisting distal ascending aorta assessment in routine echocardiography.

title: Deep learning pulmonary vessel segmentation for contrast-enhanced and non-contrast CT images.
abstract: Background Accurate and comprehensive segmentation of pulmonary vasculature is essential for diagnosing various pulmonary diseases and lung surgical planning. Purpose To develop a deep learning model for pulmonary vessels segmentation based on both computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) and non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) data, and to evaluate its performance on a clinical dataset. Methods In this retrospective study, we collected 427 cases of chest CT data from different countries and manufacturers, including 213 CTPA cases and 214 NCCT cases. And we designed a CTPA and NCCT ground truth (GT) generation method producing high-accuracy vessel annotation dataset. Then we developed a 3D U-Net based deep learning method with the Vessel Lumen Structure Optimization Module (VLSOM). We numerically evaluated model using metrics including Centerline Recall (Cl-Recall), Centerline DICE (Cl-DICE), Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD) and 95% Hausdorff Distance (HD95) focusing on the integrity of vascular structures. Finally, the model performance was visually assessed in an independent external dataset. Results In the numerical evaluation on the internal test dataset with 57 cases, our model achieved Cl-DICE, Cl-Recall and HD95 values of 0.909 (95% CI [0.904, 0.914]), 0.883 (95% CI [0.873, 0.891]) and 1.861 mm (95% CI [1.674 mm, 2.073 mm]) which is superior to the state of the art (SOTA) baseline model nnU-Net v2 of 0.860 (95% CI [0.852, 0.867]), 0.772 (95% CI [0.760, 0.783])and 2.458 mm (95% CI [2.219 mm, 2.708 mm]) (all p < 0.001). In the clinical visual assessments on the 90 sets of external datasets, the average score for accuracy and robustness, branch abundance, computer-aided detection and vascular continuity 4.52 (95% CI [4.42, 4.62]), 4.82 (95% CI [4.76, 4.90]), 4.58 (95% CI [4.46, 4.69]), and 4.85 (95% CI [4.77, 4.92]) respectively with a full score of 5. Conclusions The proposed pulmonary vessel segmentation algorithm performed well in preserving the connectivity and integrity of the vascular structure on both CTPA and NCCT data with various diseases. Critical relevance statement A vessel centerline topology-enhanced deep segmentation model enables accurate and automatic pulmonary vessel segmentation in both computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) and non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) images.

title: Characterization of local linearity in deep learning CT denoising networks.
abstract: Background Deep learning algorithms for image processing have been proposed for a wide range of applications. In particular, deep learning CT denoising has demonstrated superior ability to reduce noise compared to conventional methods. However, the nonlinear nature of these algorithms makes it difficult to inspect and visualize how the model accomplishes the denoising task. Purpose We propose a local linearization approach to characterize and analyze the behavior of deep learning algorithms. Example analysis was performed for a classic denoising architecture with convolutional neural network and ReLU activation functions, and was extended to GELU activation and a transformer-based architecture. Methods We defined strictly local linear regions as the input space over which the activation patterns of all ReLU activation functions are the same. The extent of these regions was investigated by perturbing clinically relevant features of a lung lesion. We further defined approximately local linear regions as the input space where Jacobians are similar and linear approximation results in small error. We developed an algorithm to partition input space over a range of lesion and background features into approximately local linear regions, and separately quantified the contribution of the noise realization and anatomical background to this approximation error. The behavior of networks trained with different levels of denoising, as well as alternative architectures, was compared. Results The extent of strictly local linear regions was found to be very small. Perturbations on the scale of 10-8mm-1 were enough to push the network to a neighboring strictly local linear region. However, the Jacobians over a large number of strictly local linear regions were found to be highly similar, which suggests that the network behaves approximately as a piecewise linear system. The partitioning algorithm identified a small number of approximately local linear regions within input spaces characterized by clinically relevant features; this number was similar for the GELU variant but increased for networks trained with more aggressive noise reduction and for a transformer-based architecture, while Jacobians transferred across anatomical backgrounds also increased approximation error. Conclusions The local linearity analysis framework can be a useful tool for elucidating the behavior of neural networks that are traditionally considered as "black-boxes." Preliminary results suggest that the framework can be applied to other differentiable architectures, subject to empirical validation, to characterize these highly nonlinear, data-dependent algorithms over input spaces of interest.

title: Free-breathing fast abdominal simultaneous T 1 , T 2 , PD and B 1 mapping via deep learning reconstruction.
abstract: Background Multi-parametric quantitative MRI (mqMRI) enables non-invasive tissue characterization and holds significant clinical value in abdominal imaging. Conventional methods are restricted by long acquisition times and motion artifacts induced by physiological processes and irregular breathing, leading to registration errors between sequential acquisitions. Purpose To develop and evaluate a framework for abdominal quantitative imaging under free-breathing conditions with reduced scan time and improved robustness to motion. Methods A novel framework integrating the longitudinal magnetization-controlled multiple overlapping-echo detachment (LMC-MOLED) sequence with synthetic data-driven deep learning reconstruction was proposed. To generate the synthetic dataset for training, a respiratory motion model combining global and local displacement vector fields was developed, ensuring temporal alignment with the inter-phase intervals of LMC-MOLED acquisitions. By applying interpolation to the original template, virtual imaging objects were generated to simulate respiratory-induced deformations while preserving anatomical textures, tissue boundaries, and inter-slice correlations. These objects were subsequently processed with MRI Bloch simulation to generate the final synthetic dataset, which was used to train a BGA-Multi-UNet architecture for motion correction and improved quantitative accuracy. Results The proposed framework enabled simultaneous mapping of T 1 , T 2 , proton density, and B 1 under free-breathing conditions. With a 5-slice interleaved acquisition, the average acquisition time was reduced to approximately one second per slice without the need for respiratory gating. Both numerical and in vivo experiments demonstrated high accuracy and repeatability, with image quality comparable to conventional breath-hold acquisitions while mitigating motion-induced artifacts. Conclusion This framework offers a rapid and reliable solution for multi-parametric abdominal imaging under free-breathing conditions. The combination of synthetic motion modeling with deep learning reconstruction enables accurate quantitative mapping with effective motion correction, offering potential clinical benefits for efficient and robust abdominal magnetic resonance imaging.

title: Biological target volume and tumor spread map: A combined approach for advanced radiotherapy targeting in glioblastoma.
abstract: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) radiotherapy planning typically applies fixed margins from the Gross Tumor Volume (GTV) to define the Clinical Target Volume (CTV) and Planning Target Volume (PTV). This standardized approach ignores patient-specific patterns of microscopic tumor spread and biological abnormalities, risking under-treatment of infiltrated tissue and unnecessary exposure of healthy brain regions. Purpose To address this limitation, we extended our novel Tumor Spread (TS) mapping approach, which models microscopic infiltration along white matter tracts to generate personalized CTVs, by incorporating a Biological Target Volume (BTV), derived from advanced diffusion and perfusion MRI, into the model. We then compared three radiation treatment planning strategies: (1) GTV with standard fixed-margin CTV and PTV, (2) GTV with a personalized CTV (pCTV G ) and PTV (PTV G ), and (3) BTV with a personalized CTV (pCTV B ) and PTV (PTV B ). Each was evaluated for feasibility of dose coverage, healthy tissue sparing, and recurrence overlap. Methods MRI data from 10 newly diagnosed GBM patients were used. BTVs were contoured using Fractional Anisotropy (FA), Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC), and relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) maps. TS maps were generated from both GTV and BTV. Virtual volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) treatment plans were created for all three strategies. We compared target volumes, organ-at-risk (OAR) doses, and spatial overlap with recurrence regions identified in follow-up imaging. Results Both pCTV G and pCTV B were consistently smaller than the standard CTV, offering reduced irradiated volume while preserving tumor coverage. The pCTV G and pCTV B spared 59% and 49% of the standard CTV margin volume, respectively. All virtual plans met clinical conformality thresholds, and mean doses to organs at risk (OARs) were lower with both personalized strategies. At follow-up, 98% of the volume of recurrent tumor was included in the standard PTV, 95% in PTV G , and 97% in PTV B . Dose coverage of ≥80% was achieved in 99% of the recurrence volume with standard PTV, and in 98% with both PTV G and PTV B . Conclusion This study demonstrated the clinical feasibility and potential dosimetric benefits of MRI-derived, biology-informed personalized target volumes for radiotherapy planning of glioblastoma patients. Among the virtual personalized strategies, the approach combining the Biological Target Volume (BTV) with Tumor Spread (TS) mapping showed reduced irradiated target volume, while improving healthy tissue sparing and spatial recurrence coverage. These findings support a shift toward individualized, biology-driven radiation planning that moves beyond the traditional GTV/CTV model.

title: A K-space guided invertible diffusion model for accelerating MRI reconstruction.
abstract: Background Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a core technology in clinical medical diagnosis, has long aimed to balance imaging quality and acquisition efficiency. Traditional MRI techniques, limited by the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, are faced with significant challenges in high-acceleration-factor imaging, including artifacts and detail loss due to sparse sampling. While existing parallel imaging, compressed sensing, and deep learning methods have improved reconstruction efficiency, they have limitations such as insufficient integration of electromagnetic physics models with biological tissue prior information, inadequate high-frequency information recovery, and high computational complexity. Purpose To address these persistent limitations in high-acceleration MRI reconstruction, this study proposes a K-space guided invertible diffusion model (KG-IDM) designed to improve reconstruction fidelity. Methods KG-IDM enables high-quality MRI reconstruction through Cross-domain Feature Injection (CFI) with Adaptive Channel-Spatial Interaction Attention (ACSIA) for multi-source feature alignment, and a K-space Guided Bimodal Spectral Enhancement Network (KG-BSEN) for dual-path frequency-spatial enhancement. This framework jointly exploits spatial and spectral representations, enhancing cross-domain feature consistency and reducing reconstruction artifacts. Results Experiments on the fastMRI single-coil knee dataset using retrospectively undersampled complex-valued k-space at 4× , 6× , 8× , and 10× acceleration show that KG-IDM achieves the highest mean PSNR and SSIM and the lowest mean NMSE relative to all nine baseline methods. At 4× acceleration, KG-IDM achieves 32.05 dB PSNR, 81.35% SSIM, and 0.0230 NMSE. At 10× , it achieves 25.58 dB, 62.55% , and 0.0815 , respectively. Paired volume-level Wilcoxon tests over 199 evaluation volumes showed statistically significant favorable differences in all 108 comparisons, with all Holm-adjusted p<10-4 . Conclusions By integrating measurement-guided cross-domain feature fusion with frequency-spatial refinement, KG-IDM consistently improves reconstruction fidelity across the evaluated acceleration factors and provides a promising framework for accelerated MRI reconstruction.

title: Dual-domain fusion unfolding network for compressed sensing MRI.
abstract: Background Compressed sensing magnetic resonance imaging (CS-MRI) aims to recover high-quality MRI images from undersampled k-space data. Deep unfolding networks (DUNs) have shown strong potential in CS-MRI due to their interpretability and reconstruction capability. However, existing methods still face two limitations: insufficient modeling of the complex-valued structure of MRI data and inadequate utilization of complementary k-space and image-domain information. These limitations may cause detail loss or noise artifacts in reconstructed images. Purpose This study aims to address these two challenges by developing a dual-domain unfolding framework that effectively integrates complementary information from the k-space and image domains for CS-MRI reconstruction. Methods This paper proposes a dual-domain fusion unfolding network (DDFU-Net) to address the aforementioned challenges by effectively integrating complementary information from the k-space and image domains. DDFU-Net introduces two core modules: the k-space reconstruction module (KRM) and the fusion attention module (FAM). The k-space reconstruction module processes complex-valued k-space data through real-imaginary decomposition and amplitude-phase representation modeling, with real-valued convolutional operations used for feature extraction. This design enables the network to exploit complementary information contained in the complex-valued k-space representation and improves detail recovery under high acceleration. The FAM promotes cross-domain interaction between the k-space and image-domain branches, enabling complementary feature fusion and improving detail restoration. A data consistency module is further incorporated to preserve the acquired k-space measurements during reconstruction. Results On the Brain and fastMRI datasets, DDFU-Net achieves competitive or superior reconstruction performance across the evaluated undersampling settings, with clear improvements in most comparisons. Ablation studies further validate the contribution of the major components. Conclusions The proposed DDFU-Net achieves strong reconstruction performance under different undersampling settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of the coordinated dual-domain reconstruction framework.

title: Development of a lung nodule volumetry tool for quality assurance assessment of low-dose lung cancer screening CT protocols.
abstract: Background Low-dose CT (LDCT) is the preferred modality for lung nodule detection and follow-up, yet standardized quality-control criteria are lacking. Volumetric accuracy is clinically important but strongly dependent on segmentation and reconstruction settings, particularly for small, low-contrast subsolid nodules, and frameworks for optimizing LDCT protocols based on volumetric performance remain limited. Purpose To develop a lung nodule segmentation and volumetry tool that evaluates volumetric accuracy across CT reconstruction settings and to demonstrate how accuracy and repeatability metrics can support protocol comparison as a quality-assurance assessment. Methods A custom semi-automatic tool was developed in Python and evaluated using the QRM Thorax phantom on a GE Revolution Apex CT system. Fifteen artificial nodules were analyzed, combining five diameters (3-12 mm) and three attenuation levels (100, -630, -800 HU). Reconstruction parameters were systematically varied, including kernel (STANDARD, LUNG), slice thickness (0.625-2.5 mm), spacing (0.625, 1.25 mm), algorithm (DLIR-H and ASiR-V at 80%), and field of view (18, 36 cm). Performance was assessed using mean relative volume error (target within ± 20%), repeatability coefficient (RC), and size-specific RMSE; the best-performing configuration per nodule type served as reference. Reconstruction effects were evaluated using factorial ANOVA, Levene's test, Welch's t-test, and bootstrap analysis with false-discovery-rate correction. Results Overall mean relative volume errors ranged from -7.1% to 6.7% for solid nodules and -14.7% to 5.8% for type 1 subsolid nodules ≥5 mm; type 2 subsolid nodules showed larger deviations (-27.1% to -12.1%). Nodule size and reconstruction kernel were the dominant contributors to mean volume error, while slice thickness and spacing mainly influenced variability. Significant differences from the reference were found for four solid-nodule settings, none for type 1, and one for type 2 subsolid settings, with degradation occurring mainly at increased slice thickness or reduced field of view. The 3 mm subsolid nodules showed consistently high variability across all settings. Conclusions The tool enabled quantitative comparison of CT reconstruction settings using volumetric accuracy and repeatability metrics. For clinically relevant sizes ( ≥5 mm), volumetric performance remained within the predefined technical-suitability range across most settings, supporting use of the tool for protocol evaluation and future dose-optimization studies.

title: Rep2Rep-Shuffle: Shuffled Repetition-to-Repetition Learning for Noise-Adaptive Self-Supervised MRI Denoising.
abstract: Purpose MRI applications with low SNR, such as non-proton imaging and low-field imaging, often require multiple signal averages to achieve adequate image quality at the cost of longer scan times. This work proposes Rep2Rep-Shuffle, a self-supervised learning framework that improves MRI denoising performance in repeated-acquisition imaging with limited training datasets. Methods Rep2Rep-Shuffle extends our previously proposed repetition-to-repetition learning (Rep2Rep)-based self-supervised denoising approach with a new shuffled repetition pairing strategy. Instead of using a fixed split between training input and target repetitions, different repetition combinations are randomly generated during training epochs for each dataset, which increases the effective training space when training datasets are limited. In addition, the framework also extends from slice-wise 2D to 3D denoising by exploiting correlations across all spatial dimensions. The proposed method was tested in vivo using sodium MRI and further validated using synthetic noisy MRI datasets. Different training strategies for both 2D and 3D denoising were compared. Results In vivo sodium MRI results demonstrated improved denoising and better preservation of anatomical structures with 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle compared with fixed pairing (Rep2Rep) and 2D denoising. Reader evaluation further confirmed that 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle received higher scores for different assessment categories. In synthetic experiments, 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle achieved the best performance among self-supervised methods and approached the performance of supervised learning. Conclusion Rep2Rep-Shuffle outperforms Rep2Rep for MRI denoising by increasing training diversity through shuffled repetition pairing and by leveraging volumetric spatial correlations. The method is particularly suited for low-SNR MRI applications that acquire multiple repetitions but have limited training datasets.
