title: Deep-Reorder: Refined Motion Correction for 3D Brain MRI via Iterative Data Regrouping.
abstract: Purpose Accurate and temporally high-resolution estimation of subject motion is paramount for effective motion-correction in MRI. This work proposes a novel approach for estimating subject motion within a 3D MRI scan with high temporal resolution. Methods Starting from an incoherent sampling scheme, images are reconstructed from temporally ordered k-space fractions via deep learning, enabling motion estimation via registration between each image. Assuming the bulk of the motion is removed using these initial estimates, the remaining misalignment between k-space fractions is expected to be minimally correlated in time. Based on this insight, an iterative strategy is proposed in which shots are arbitrarily regrouped into new k-space fractions, regardless of their original temporal ordering, for subsequent motion estimation and correction. This effectively increases the temporal resolution of the approach, enabling individual correction of all shots. Results When applied to 3D T1w TFE MRI of the brain, the proposed approach "Deep-Reorder" estimated a unique motion state for all shots, producing significantly better estimations of retrospective motion compared to estimation without iterative data regrouping. On prospectively motion-corrupted scans with intentional head movement by volunteers, the proposed approach consistently improved image quality, producing less noisy images with reduced motion artifacts. Conclusion In conclusion, the proposed approach, which is free of external tracking devices or navigators, effectively estimated 3D motion and corrected motion artifacts with increased temporal resolution.

title: Adaptive Mask-Guided k-Space Diffusion for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction.
abstract: Purpose Masked modeling has emerged as a powerful deep learning paradigm that reconstructs missing data by predicting masked regions, achieving strong performance across multiple domains. As a critical task in medical imaging, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction aims to recover high-quality images from under-sampled k-space data. However, existing methods usually optimize the full image domain or k-space, while overlooking the importance and structural roles of different frequency components. Methods An adaptive mask-guided diffusion model (AMDM) was developed, which leverages adaptively estimated frequency distributions from k-space to construct a hybrid mask mechanism for handling diverse k-space inputs. It enables the effective separation of high-frequency and low-frequency components, producing multiple prior representations. In addition, the frequency distribution is used to generate adaptive masks, which subsequently guide the closed-loop diffusion process. Results Experimental results demonstrated improved reconstruction performance through frequency-aware modeling. AMDM achieved a PSNR of 36.89 dB on an independent public brain dataset without retraining, even at an under-sampling factor of R=12 . Conclusion The proposed method shows that explicitly modeling k-space frequency heterogeneity provides an effective prior for MRI reconstruction, offering a promising direction for robust reconstruction under aggressive under-sampling.

title: Combining Cartesian and Non-Cartesian Acceleration Techniques With SPARKLING for 1 mm Isotropic Whole-Brain MPRAGE in a Minute.
abstract: Purpose T1 -weighted MPRAGE remains a cornerstone of clinical anatomical imaging, yet its long acquisition times constrain routine use. Established acceleration techniques, namely Parallel Imaging (PI) and Compressed Sensing (CS), tend to introduce substantial noise and blurring when pushed to high acceleration factors. Although they rely on fundamentally different redundancies, combining them synergistically remains an open challenge. Methods The GoLF-SPARKLING framework was extended to jointly exploit two acceleration mechanisms: PI-based uniform undersampling in the central k-space region and variable-density CS at the periphery, with independent acceleration factors in each zone. To preserve smooth signal evolution throughout the inversion-recovery period and avoid modulation artifacts, the acquisition trajectory was reordered accordingly. The resulting method was evaluated prospectively in vivo at 1 mm isotropic resolution and benchmarked against Wave-CAIPI and Poisson-disk sampling as respective PI and CS baselines. Results The proposed hybrid approach produced sharper, less noisy, and more stable whole-brain images in approximately 1 min than either acceleration strategy alone. Purely PI-based reconstructions were degraded by high g-factor noise, while exclusively CS-based reconstructions exhibited pronounced blurring. Furthermore, this method yielded lower average volumetric errors in downstream automated brain segmentation than state-of-the-art acceleration techniques, demonstrating its clinical utility. Conclusion By jointly leveraging PI and CS, GoLF-SPARKLING achieves high acceleration factors that enable sub-minute, high-quality anatomical MRI. This translates into greater clinical throughput and more reliable imaging in patients who are challenging to scan.

title: Liver T1, T2, T2*, and PDFF Mapping at 0.55 T Using Rosette MRF With Optimized Sequence Design and Deep Image Reconstruction.
abstract: Purpose Quantitative imaging on mid-field (0.55 T) MRI systems can suffer from poor precision due to low SNR. This work presents an MRF pulse sequence optimized with Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) and combined with a multi-echo deep image prior (DIP) reconstruction for co-registered T1/T2/T2*/PDFF mapping in the liver at 0.55 T within a single breath-hold. Methods A 20 s 2D multi-echo rosette MRF breath-hold acquisition was implemented on a 0.55 T wide-bore system. The sequence design was optimized via pseudorandom search using a CRLB-based objective for T1/T2 encoding and compared with reference designs. Data were reconstructed using (i) an iterative low-rank (LR) reconstruction and (ii) a multi-echo DIP jointly modeling TR- and echo-domain dynamics including B0 effects. title: Fast Voxelwise SNR Estimation for Iterative MRI Reconstructions.
abstract: Purpose To develop a fast, general-purpose framework for voxelwise noise characterization in iterative MRI reconstructions, recovering the image-domain noise variance, the primary quantity from which SNR, g -factor, and related image-quality metrics are derived. The framework addresses both the intractability of closed-form formulas beyond Cartesian sampling and the long runtime of pseudo multiple replica (PMR). Methods A stochastic noise estimator is proposed that operates in the image domain by Probing the Image-space noise COvariance matrix (PICO) with random probe images. Complex random-phase probes attain minimum kurtosis and reduce estimator variance in the tested reconstruction. PICO was validated against analytical benchmarks and PMR references using Cartesian knee data ( R=2 ), physical brain phantom data ( R=2,3,4 ), in vivo non-Cartesian brain data ( R=2 ), and compressed-sensing knee reconstructions ( R=2 ). Results In Cartesian reconstructions, PICO accurately reproduced analytical SENSE g -factor maps. In non-Cartesian reconstructions, it achieved 1% g -factor NRMSE ≈11.9× faster than PMR in a phantom and ≈2.81× faster in vivo, with the efficiency advantage persisting at higher acceleration. For compressed sensing, the Jacobian-based estimator produced noise maps consistent with PMR and computed them 1.84× faster at equal sample counts. Agreement worsened at large added-noise amplitudes and moderate TV strengths. Conclusion PICO targets the exact covariance of fixed linear reconstructions and a first-order covariance for nonlinear reconstructions, providing a computationally efficient alternative to PMR. By reusing existing reconstruction primitives, it could help incorporate voxelwise noise maps into reconstruction workflows.

title: Quantitative Analysis of Muscle Ultrasound Images in Adult Patients With Pompe Disease Using Radiomics.
abstract: Introduction/aims Pompe disease is a genetic myopathy caused by acid alpha-glucosidase enzyme deficiency. Treatment response is mainly evaluated using motor scores, for instance the 6-min walk test (6MWT) or the Motor Function Measure-32 (MFM-32), which can be time-consuming and biased by fatigue and motivation. Quantitative muscle ultrasound may be an additional biomarker for monitoring disease progression. Our objective was to study the performance of a large number of quantitative features derived from muscle ultrasound images to predict motor involvement in late-onset Pompe disease. Methods We retrospectively collected muscle ultrasound images from 19 patients with late-onset Pompe disease and 28 control subjects, and calculated 93 quantitative features for each image. Using a radiomics approach, we selected reproducible features that were significantly different between patients and controls, and then assessed their predictive power for the 6MWT and the MFM-32 score. Results Among the 93 features, 36 (38.7%) showed good reproducibility, and 18 (19.3%) were significantly different between Pompe patients and controls after adjustment for age, sex, and body mass index. The most predictive features of motor functions were the grayscale 10th percentile in the rectus femoris, biceps brachii, deltoid, and extensor carpi radialis muscles, explaining 76% of the variance of the 6MWT, and 84% of the variance of the MFM-32 score. Discussion These findings confirm the association between muscle ultrasound and motor function in Pompe disease found by previous studies and suggest that radiomics can identify additional predictive features, such as the grayscale 10th percentile.

title: Synthetic Data in MR Spectroscopy: Current Practices, Applications, and Considerations.
abstract: Synthetic data generation has become an increasingly important component of methodological development in magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), particularly in contexts where ground-truth in vivo measurements are limited, noisy, or inaccessible. This review provides a structured overview of current practices in synthetic MRS data generation, with emphasis on the physical, biochemical, and computational assumptions that underpin commonly used models. A decomposition of synthetic MRS data is presented in terms of core building blocks, including basis sets, signal formation models, and metabolite parameter distributions such as concentration and relaxation properties. This framework is extended to advanced components required for realistic data synthesis, including baseline and nuisance signals, spatial encoding effects such as coil sensitivities and field inhomogeneities, k-space sampling and gradient imperfections, as well as sample-specific and temporal dynamics. Beyond single-voxel modeling, synthetic data generation across multiple MRS modalities is discussed, including functional MRS, diffusion-weighted MRS, and spectroscopic imaging, with emphasis on modality-specific challenges such as physiological variability, motion, and confounding signal contributions. The role of synthetic data in clinical and preclinical research, acquisition optimization, software validation, and emerging artificial intelligence applications is further examined, with particular attention to domain shift and representational realism. Current practices in validation, reporting standards, and data accessibility are also reviewed, and key gaps limiting reproducibility and interoperability across studies are identified. Overall, this work provides a unified conceptual framework for synthetic MRS data generation, clarifies underlying assumptions across modeling choices, and outlines open challenges toward improving realism, standardization, and utility in both methodological and translational applications. Conducted by the MRS Synthetic Data Working Group under the Code & Data Sharing Committee of the MRS Study Group of the International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine (ISMRM), this review encompasses the existing literature, supplemented by the collective experience and in-house methodologies of its contributors, providing a community perspective that extends beyond the published record.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Magnetic Resonance Elastography Versus Vibration-Controlled Transient Elastography for Liver Fibrosis Staging in Steatotic Liver Disease.
abstract: Gravitational magnetic resonance elastography (GT-MRE) enables comprehensive biomechanical liver characterization and may overcome limitations of conventional elastography techniques. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) GT-MRE compared with 2D acoustic MRE (AC-MRE) and vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) for liver fibrosis staging. In this prospective study, patients with suspected or known steatotic liver disease underwent GT-MRE (2D and 3D, gradient-echo sequences) and AC-MRE (2D, spin-echo echo-planar imaging) at 1.5 T, plus VCTE with a median interval to MRE of 37 days (IQR, 20-124 days; range, 0-372 days). Statistical analyses included generalized additive models, ordinal logistic regression, and decision tree-based classification. Diagnostic performance was assessed using cumulative receiver operating characteristic analysis and corresponding areas under the curve (AUCs). Ninety-one participants (median age, 55 years [IQR, 45-64]; 41 women) were included, of whom 35 (38%) had histopathological correlation. In the biopsy-confirmed subgroup, 3D GT-MRE-derived viscoelastic parameters showed promising exploratory performance for early fibrosis classification. Wave attenuation achieved AUCs of 0.91 for F0 versus ≥ F1 and 0.99 for ≤ F1 versus ≥ F2, while phase angle yielded an AUC of 0.88 for F0 versus ≥ F1, with numerically higher AUCs than conventional stiffness-based metrics. For advanced fibrosis thresholds, all modalities performed well (AUC ≥ 0.84). Obuchowski measures for 3D-derived parameters were 0.95-0.96. Internally cross-validated multiparametric modeling achieved an accuracy of up to 92%. VCTE measurements plateaued beyond F3, whereas AC- and GT-MRE metrics continued to increase with fibrosis severity. 3D GT-MRE-derived viscoelastic parameters showed promising performance for liver fibrosis classification and provided biomechanical information complementary to conventional stiffness measurements. Given the limited biopsy-confirmed sample and marked class imbalance at F0, these findings require validation in larger independent cohorts before clinical implementation.

title: 2D U-Net Framework for Multiclass Automated Segmentation of Healthy Structures, Ischemic Stroke, and Glioblastoma in the Rat Brain.
abstract: Rodents are essential for preclinical brain disease research, including stroke, tumors, and neurodegenerative disorders. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables longitudinal brain tissue visualization, but accurate segmentation is crucial for meaningful analysis. This study introduces a multitask 2D U-Net, a convolutional neural network designed for automated segmentation and quantification of brain regions, ischemic stroke lesions, and tumors in rats using T 2 -weighted imaging (T 2 -wi) and T 2 -relaxation maps. The model was evaluated on the following three MRI datasets: (i) segmentation of multiple brain regions in healthy rats, (ii) ischemic stroke lesions using T 2 -relaxation maps, and (iii) glioblastoma tumors using T 2 -wi. Performance was assessed using the Dice coefficient (DC), Hausdorff distance (HD), sensitivity (SEN), and volume ratio (VR), comparing network outputs against semiautomatic ground truths and existing models. A total of 1949 images from 111 rats were analyzed, expanded to 5847 through data augmentation. After correcting an animal-level train/test partitioning that prevented data leakage between subjects, the model achieved robust accuracy across all tasks (DC = 0.80-0.96, HD = 0.83-2.16 mm, SEN = 0.75-0.96, VR = 0.89-1.10), showing a strong correlation ( ρ=0.82-0.99 ) with manual annotations. This framework improves segmentation accuracy, robustness, and applicability across different MRI settings and conditions, addressing issues like interrater variability and time inefficiency when analyzing rodent brain MRI data. Datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NOBEL-MRI/Rat-Datasets.

title: The Associations Between Olfactory Bulb Morphology, Volume Change, and Olfactory Recovery.
abstract: Objective To investigate whether olfactory bulb (OB) morphology is associated with olfactory recovery following olfactory training (OT) in individuals with COVID-19-related smell loss. Study design Prospective observational study. Setting University hospital and research center. Methods Twenty women with COVID-19-associated olfactory dysfunction and 19 healthy controls underwent OT for 3 months. OB shape (oval vs non-oval) was classified using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and bilateral OB volumes were manually segmented before and after OT. Olfactory performance was assessed with the Sniffin' Sticks test. Statistical analyses included independent t tests, multimodal analysis of covariance, correlation analyses, and generalized estimating equations. Results At baseline, OB volume correlated significantly with olfactory performance. Changes in left OB volume were positively correlated with changes in odor threshold. Following OT, patients with non-oval OB shapes showed greater improvement in Threshold + Discrimination + Identification (TDI) scores and enlargement of left OB volume compared to those with oval-shaped OB. However, OB morphology did not significantly change over time in both patients and controls. Conclusion OB shape may provide a novel perspective for predicting prognosis after OT. Further studies with larger cohorts and extended training durations are warranted to validate these preliminary observations.

title: Prognostic Predictors in Patients With Necrotizing Otitis Externa: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Objective Necrotizing otitis externa (NOE) is a rare infection with a heterogeneous clinical course that complicates prognostication. The impact of diabetes mellitus on outcomes remains controversial, and objective predictors of treatment duration are unclear. This study aimed to identify the factors associated with prolonged hospitalization in patients with NOE. Study design Retrospective observational study. Setting Tertiary academic medical center. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 61 patients with NOE admitted between September 2009 and October 2024. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, microbiological, and radiological data, as well as length of hospital stay, were analyzed. Magnetic resonance imaging assessed skull-base osteomyelitis and white matter lesions using the Fazekas scale. Multivariable linear regression identified factors associated with hospital stay. Results The mean age was 70.25 ± 13.11 years (63.9% male; mean hospital stay 46.02 ± 37.50 days). Diabetes was present in 75.4% of the patients, but neither diabetes nor hemoglobin A1c levels were associated with hospital stay. In the univariate analysis, diabetic complications, external auditory canal swelling, cranial nerve palsy, peak inflammatory marker levels, inflammatory marker normalization times, and higher Fazekas scores were associated with prolonged hospitalization, whereas only diabetic complications and higher Fazekas scores remained independently associated in the multivariable analysis (adjusted R 2 = 0.425). Conclusion Diabetic complications and higher Fazekas scores were independently associated with prolonged hospitalization in patients with NOE. These findings suggest that chronic microvascular disease burden, rather than conventional vascular risk factors alone, may contribute to a prolonged disease course. Further prospective multicenter studies are needed to validate these findings.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Supraclavicular Brachiocephalic Vein Cannulation in Pediatric Patients With Hematological Disorders: A Retrospective Comparative Study.
abstract: Background Central venous access is indispensable for clinical management of pediatric patients with hematological disorders, including chemotherapy administration, blood product transfusion, and critical rescue. Repeated venipuncture attempts, procedural failure, postoperative catheter malposition, and cannulation-related complications can substantially disrupt subsequent treatment courses and compromise therapeutic efficacy. Aims This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and safety of ultrasound-guided brachiocephalic vein (BCV) cannulation, with the goal of optimizing central venous catheterization protocols, reducing procedure-related adverse events, and improving the efficiency and safety of treatment via central venous access in pediatric patients. Methods This retrospective study included 580 children (303 subclavian vein [SCV], 277 BCV) who underwent ultrasound-guided central venous catheterization between January 2021 and December 2024. We compared first-attempt success rate, overall success rate, procedural duration, intraoperative adverse events, postoperative complications, and catheter malposition. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to improve comparability between the groups with respect to measured baseline covariates. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent risk factors. Results After IPTW, the BCV approach was associated with a higher first-attempt success rate (OR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.05-2.81; risk difference [RD] = 0.119, 95% CI: 0.015-0.222) and a higher overall success rate (RD = 0.091, 95% CI: 0.013-0.168). The mean procedural duration was 6 min shorter in the BCV group (95% CI: -9.5 to -2.5). The BCV approach was independently associated with lower odds of intraoperative malposition (OR = 0.096, 95% CI: 0.037-0.249), postoperative malposition (OR = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.16-0.74), and perioperative complications (OR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.08-0.94). Multivariable regression analysis showed that catheterization approach was independently associated with catheter malposition. Background

Central venous access is indispensable for clinical management of pediatric patients with hematological disorders, including chemotherapy administration, blood product transfusion, and critical rescue. Repeated venipuncture attempts, procedural failure, postoperative catheter malposition, and cannulation-related complications can substantially disrupt subsequent treatment courses and compromise therapeutic efficacy.

Aims

This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and safety of ultrasound-guided brachiocephalic vein (BCV) cannulation, with the goal of optimizing central venous catheterization protocols, reducing procedure-related adverse events, and improving the efficiency and safety of treatment via central venous access in pediatric patients.

Compared with SCV, ultrasound-guided BCV cannulation is associated with higher success rates, shorter procedural duration, and fewer malpositions and complications. This technique may offer particular benefits for children with hematological disorders.

title: Spatial transcriptomics reveal depth-dependent nerve growth factor and M2-like macrophage enrichment in the perineural invasion of distal cholangiocarcinoma.
abstract: Perineural invasion (PNI) is a frequent pathological feature of distal cholangiocarcinoma. The spatial molecular programs associated with PNI are unclear. We aimed to characterize tumor-nerve-immune interactions linked to PNI using spatial transcriptomics and independent validation. Spatial transcriptomics was performed using GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiler on six cases of surgically resected distal cholangiocarcinoma (non-PNI, n = 3; PNI, n = 3). Regions of interest included non-PNI tumor regions, surface mucosal tumor regions without neural contact (PNI-surface), and tumor regions adjacent to S100-positive nerves (PNI-perineural). Tumor compartments were enriched by CK19-based segmentation. Differential expression and pathway analyses were performed using iDEP/DESeq2 and Reactome/Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment. Validation at the protein level was conducted using immunohistochemistry in an independent cohort (non-PNI, n = 22 and PNI, n = 82) for nerve growth factor (NGF), CD68, and CD163. Three-dimensional nerve architecture was assessed in nine additional cases using tissue clearing. PNI-associated compartments and non-PNI regions had distinct transcriptional profiles. Compared to that in non-PNI, 109 genes were differentially expressed in PNI-surface (34 up- and 75 downregulated) and 179 in PNI-perineural (64 up- and 115 downregulated). Pathway analyses identified enrichment of immune-, microenvironment-, and neurotrophic-related programs, including NGF-associated signatures. Tumor-cell NGF expression was significantly higher in PNI-positive tumors (median H-score: 215 versus 119, p < 0.0001) and increased with depth in PNI cases (p < 0.0001). Deep invasive regions of PNI-positive tumors saw a significant increase in CD68-positive (median 313 versus 210 cells per high-power field, p < 0.001) and CD163-positive (median 64 versus 40 cells per high-power field, p < 0.01) macrophages. CD163/CD68 ratio increased in deep versus surface regions, specifically in PNI-positive tumors (p < 0.0001). PNI-positive distal cholangiocarcinoma exhibited spatially distinct tumor programs and depth-dependent remodeling involving NGF upregulation and M2-like macrophage enrichment, identifying potential therapeutic targets. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Observing Skepticism Toward a Breast Cancer Screening Decision Aid Over Time.
abstract: Objective Prior research reported that some women are skeptical toward messages about mammography screening evidence, particularly information about overdiagnosis and false positives. The proposed cause of skepticism is that the evidence is surprising and different from other screening messages, a finding which suggests that skepticism might decline as the information becomes more familiar. The present research tested the hypothesis that skepticism declines over time with repeated exposure, and sought to replicate prior evidence for the antecedents of observed skepticism. Methods This longitudinal study recruited women ages 39-49 from two health systems. Women received a decision aid (DA) communicating mammography screening evidence prior to an annual well visit. Skepticism toward the DA information was measured immediately after the DA, after the clinic visit, and 3 months later. Hypothesis-relevant predictors of skepticism were assessed. Results Skepticism was greater toward information about overdiagnosis and false positives compared to benefits, and skepticism was greater among participants who felt the evidence conflicted with past screening messages. We also observed that higher breast cancer anxiety was associated skepticism toward screening harms. Moreover, contrary to predictions, two facets of skepticism-reactance and disbelief-increased over time. Exploratory post hoc analyses suggested that increases in skepticism were associated with participants' perceptions that the DA conflicted with their doctors' screening message. Conclusions Some people express skepticism toward mammography evidence, and these feelings are associated with perceived conflicting messages and cancer anxiety. Skepticism may not decline over time if messages from other sources conflict with the DA information. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov registration NCT05838417.

title: Thoracic Endometriosis Mimicking a Lung Mass: Management With Single-Stage Biopsy and Microwave Ablation.
abstract: Thoracic endometriosis syndrome is a rare extrapelvic manifestation involving the pleura, diaphragm or lung parenchyma. Presentation as a solitary pulmonary nodule mimicking malignancy is uncommon. We report a 31-year-old asymptomatic woman with an enlarging right lower lobe nodule, measuring 1.8-2.1 cm over 3 months. Following shared decision-making, single-stage image-guided biopsy and microwave ablation (MWA) were performed. Histopathology confirmed pulmonary endometriosis. No clinically significant postoperative complications occurred, and the patient was discharged on postoperative Day 1. Follow-up CT at 6 and 12 months demonstrated no obvious local recurrence without additional treatment. This case describes a potential minimally invasive approach for selected pulmonary lesions, although the safety, efficacy and long-term outcomes of MWA for pulmonary endometriosis remain uncertain.

title: Diagnostic Challenges in Paediatric Pulmonary Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma: A Case Report.
abstract: Paediatric lung nodules pose a diagnostic challenge due to a broad differential diagnosis and limited standardized evaluation guidelines. We present the case of a 12-year-old female with an incidentally discovered 27 mm calcified left pulmonary nodule during evaluation for chronic cough. She was asymptomatic at presentation, with an unremarkable examination and an extensive negative infectious, oncologic, and rheumatologic workup. Procedural challenges due to the proximity to the airway hilum, along with limited access to paediatric bronchoscopic expertise, necessitated multi-institutional coordination for surgical biopsy. Histopathology confirmed pulmonary mucoepidermoid carcinoma (PMEC), followed by lobectomy with negative margins and an excellent prognosis. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of paediatric lung nodules and the importance of multidisciplinary and cross-institutional coordination when procedural feasibility and specialized expertise limit diagnostic approach.

title: Tunable 18 F-Labeling of Erlotinib-Based Small Molecule Nanodrugs for Rapid PET Imaging and Targeted Therapy.
abstract: Small molecule nanodrugs (SMNs) offer unique advantages for cancer therapy, yet accurately tracking their in vivo fate without perturbing their native assembly remains challenging. Here, we report a spacer engineering strategy that enables efficient 1 8 F-labeling while preserving SMNs self-assembly. Erlotinib-based amphiphilic derivatives containing oligoethylene glycol (OEG) spacers of tunable length were designed to simultaneously regulate steric hindrance for aliphatic S N 2 radiofluorination and the amphiphilic balance required for nanoparticle formation. Spacer elongation reduced steric hindrance at the labeling site and thereby improved radiochemical yields, while also enabling precise control over nanoparticle size. The optimized radiolabeled formulation, [ 18 F]E3F NPs , exhibited prolonged blood circulation and rapid tumor accumulation, enabling high-contrast PET imaging of PANC-1 xenografts as early as 15 min after injection. In addition, the corresponding nonradioactive formulation, E3F NPs , showed significantly improved antitumor efficacy compared with nonassembled E3F through reduced EGFR phosphorylation and increased tumor cell apoptosis. This work provides an initial evaluation that spacer engineering can coordinate radiolabeling and self-assembly while enabling PET tracking of SMNs, supporting the development of image-guided cancer theranostics.

title: Classification of brain variants on fetal ultrasound: international Delphi consensus.
abstract: Objective To develop an expert consensus classification and management framework for fetal-brain variants identified on prenatal ultrasound across all trimesters of pregnancy that cannot be categorized confidently as either benign or pathological. Methods A two-round international Delphi survey was conducted among experts in fetal medicine and neurosonography, with survey data collected between September 2025 and March 2026. Forty-eight fetal-brain variants, identified through a scoping literature review of PubMed/MEDLINE from database inception to August 2025, performed between June and August 2025, and illustrated with representative ultrasound images, were evaluated. Brain variants were classified according to clinical significance and recommended management into three predefined categories: 'green' (benign variants requiring no additional investigation or follow-up), 'orange' (requiring neurosonographic follow-up) and 'red' (requiring dedicated neurosonography, fetal-brain magnetic resonance imaging and/or genetic investigations). Consensus was predefined as ≥ 70% agreement. In Round 2, experts confirmed their agreement regarding categorization of variants that had reached consensus in Round 1 and reassessed variants that did not reach initial consensus. Results Forty-eight experts from 14 countries participated in Round 1 and 39 (81.3%) completed both rounds. Of the 48 evaluated variants, 35 (72.9%) reached consensus after two rounds: 12 were classified as 'green', seven as 'orange' and 16 as 'red'. Green variants included isolated choroid plexus cysts < 10 mm across all trimesters, regular asymmetry of the choroid plexuses, isolated cavum septations, cavum vergae, cavum velum interpositum, isolated small cavum septi pellucidi with intact corpus callosum and dolichocephaly with normal head circumference and normal brain morphology. Orange variants included isolated enlargement of intracranial translucency with preserved anatomy, large or bilateral choroid plexus cysts, isolated enlargement of subarachnoid spaces without compression and isolated cyst of the cavum septi pellucidi. Red variants included abnormal posterior fossa markers (loss of normal three-space anatomy, increased brainstem-vermis angle, reduced brainstem-occipital bone distance), periventricular cysts associated with adjacent white-matter abnormalities, thickened corpus callosum and distortion of the interhemispheric fissure, among other findings. Thirteen (27.1%) variants failed to reach consensus, highlighting persistent uncertainty in interpreting subtle isolated asymmetries and selected cystic variants. Conclusions This international Delphi consensus proposes an initial expert-derived classification of commonly encountered feta-brain variants on ultrasound. Because the classification has not been validated against postnatal imaging or neurodevelopmental outcomes and reproducibility has not been assessed, prospective evaluation is required before it can be applied in routine practice. © 2026 International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology.

title: Early third-trimester maternal cardiac function and morphometry in high-risk pregnancies that subsequently developed fetal growth restriction and/or pre-eclampsia.
abstract: Objective To evaluate maternal cardiovascular function and cardiac morphology in early third-trimester pregnancies at high risk for fetal growth restriction (FGR) and compare findings between pregnancies that subsequently developed FGR and/or pre-eclampsia (PE) and uncomplicated pregnancies. Methods This prospective cohort study included singleton pregnancies at high risk for FGR referred to the Maternal-Fetal Medicine Department at the Hospital Clinic of Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain, between August 2022 and August 2024, for a routine second-trimester fetal anomaly scan. The patients were assessed between 27 + 0 and 28 + 6 weeks' gestation and were only included in the analysis if they did not have a diagnosis of FGR or PE at the time of evaluation; those who subsequently developed FGR and/or PE were identified during follow-up. Maternal echocardiography was performed to assess cardiac output (CO), stroke volume (SV), systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and structural parameters including left ventricular (LV) wall thickness and chamber volumes. Results were compared between pregnancies that subsequently developed FGR (with or without PE), pregnancies that subsequently developed isolated PE and uncomplicated pregnancies. Multivariable analysis was performed using quantile regression of the medians for CO and SVR, adjusted for body mass index (BMI), with FGR and PE assessed independently. Results A total of 948 patients were included in the final analysis, of whom 129 developed FGR and/or PE (including 59 that developed FGR (with or without PE) and 70 that developed isolated PE) and 819 had uncomplicated pregnancies. Median mean arterial pressure (MAP) was higher in the FGR (with or without PE) group (82.0 mmHg) and the isolated-PE group (84.8 mmHg) than in the uncomplicated group (79.7 mmHg; P = 0.027 and P < 0.001, respectively), with the isolated-PE group showing the highest MAP values (isolated PE vs FGR (with or without PE), P = 0.047). Median heart rate was elevated in the isolated-PE group (82.5 bpm) compared with the FGR (with or without PE) group (77.0 bpm; P = 0.03). In the multivariable analysis, FGR and PE were associated independently with lower CO and higher SVR prior to their development. Median SV was reduced in the FGR (with or without PE) group (59.7 mL) and the isolated-PE group (61.1 mL) compared with the uncomplicated group (64.2 mL; P = 0.030 and P = 0.016, respectively). Median BMI-indexed CO was also lower in the FGR (with or without PE) group (0.18 (L/min)/(kg/m 2 )) and the isolated-PE group (0.17 (L/min)/(kg/m 2 )) compared with the uncomplicated group (0.19 (L/min)/(kg/m 2 ); P = 0.005 and P = 0.001, respectively). Median SVR was elevated in the FGR (with or without PE) group (1393 dynes × s/cm 5 ) and the isolated-PE group (1339 dynes × s/cm 5 ) compared with the uncomplicated group (1252 dynes × s/cm 5 ; P < 0.001 and P = 0.01, respectively). Compared with the uncomplicated group, the isolated-PE group showed greater median LV myocardial thickness at end diastole (0.50 vs 0.47 cm; P = 0.003), interventricular septal thickness at end diastole (0.92 vs 0.89 cm; P = 0.031), posterior wall thickness at end diastole (0.98 vs 0.94 cm; P = 0.013) and relative wall thickness (0.45 vs 0.42; P = 0.001). Moreover, the FGR (with or without PE) group had a smaller median LV end-diastolic diameter (4.27 cm) compared with the uncomplicated group (4.48 cm; P = 0.003), indicating that preload may be reduced in patients who developed FGR (with or without PE). LV mass indexed for BMI was similar across groups. Conclusions Maternal cardiovascular alterations may precede the development of FGR and PE and differ by phenotype. Pregnancies that subsequently developed FGR and/or PE showed reduced CO, but those that developed FGR reflected lower preload without tachycardia, while those that developed isolated PE showed hypertensive features with a compensatory rise in heart rate. Maternal echocardiography may aid early risk stratification and guide tailored surveillance and therapy in pregnancies at high risk for FGR. © 2026 International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology.

title: Predicting Blood Flow in Reconstructed Intestines Based on Abdominal Aortic Calcification and Clinical Effects of Left Colic Artery Preservation in Colorectal Cancer Surgery: A Subanalysis of the HiSCO-09 Study.
abstract: Aim To clarify the relationship between the abdominal aortic calcification score on preoperative computed tomography and intraoperative regional tissue oxygen saturation (rSO 2 ), assess the feasibility of predicting perfusion impairment through imaging, and evaluate whether left colic artery preservation improves blood flow and reduces the risk of anastomotic leakage in patients with impaired perfusion. Methods In this subanalysis of the HiSCO-09 trial, rSO 2 was measured using INVOS in the intestinal segment at the intended intestinal anastomosis site following mesenteric preparation as a blood flow indicator. Patients were categorized according to the abdominal aortic calcification score based on preoperative computed tomography findings into low (≤ 2.13 mL) and high (> 2.13 mL) groups. Results Of the 282 patients, the high abdominal aortic calcification group included 135 patients. Compared with the low group, the high group showed significantly higher incidence of anastomotic leakage (4.8% vs. 12.6%, p = 0.019) and consistently lower rSO 2 values. Abdominal aortic calcification score correlated negatively with rSO 2 at the anastomosis site (p = 0.011). Within the high group, left colic artery preservation was associated with higher rSO 2 and a lower incidence of anastomotic leakage (p = 0.032). Conclusions Preoperative abdominal aortic calcification assessment was weakly associated with reduced intraoperative rSO 2 . Exploratory subgroup analysis indicated that left colic artery preservation was associated with better perfusion and fewer anastomotic leakages in patients with high calcification. Although insufficient as a stand-alone predictor, abdominal aortic calcification may serve as a complementary factor in multifactorial preoperative risk assessments for future prospective evaluation.

title: Advanced Diffusion MRI in the Human Brain: Microstructure Imaging and Structural Connectivity.
abstract: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) is one of the most powerful MRI techniques for exploring the brain's microstructure in vivo. By measuring how water molecules move within tissue, it provides unique insight into the cellular and fiber architecture of the brain-information that conventional MRI cannot reveal. In clinical settings, diffusion imaging is now a valuable tool for early stroke diagnosis, tumour characterization, and surgical planning. In research, it enables the study of brain development, ageing, and disease progression, linking imaging findings to cellular and molecular processes. Over the past three decades, diffusion MRI has evolved from simple diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps to advanced models that capture the complexity of tissue organization. Techniques such as diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), diffusional kurtosis imaging (DKI), and multi-compartment biophysical models now allow estimation of parameters related to axonal density, myelination, and water exchange between cellular compartments. Combined with tractography, these methods enable noninvasive reconstruction of white-matter pathways and network-level connectivity, transforming dMRI into a central tool for both neuroscience and clinical use. This chapter introduces the principles and applications of diffusion MRI in a progressive manner. We begin with the fundamental physics of diffusion contrast and its clinical relevance, then move to advanced microstructural models that provide richer biological specificity. Subsequent sections describe tractography methods used to map brain connectivity and analyze structural networks. Together, these sections aim to provide readers, especially those with limited imaging background, with an accessible understanding of how diffusion MRI reveals the brain's hidden microstructure and connects it to biological function.

title: Medical Imaging Analysis of X-Ray, MRI, and CT Scans for Clinical Diagnostics.
abstract: This chapter focuses on the clinical applications of three mainstream medical imaging modalities-X-ray, CT, and MRI-providing a systematic analysis of their imaging mechanisms, typical indications, strengths, and limitations. The diagnostic performance of each modality is compared across various disease scenarios. With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), medical imaging analysis is advancing toward greater intelligence and standardization. Deep learning-based techniques for image recognition and lesion segmentation have significantly improved diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. Meanwhile, emerging technologies such as multimodal image fusion, remote collaborative reading, and radiomics are expanding the clinical boundaries of medical imaging. These innovations have found broad applications across the nervous, respiratory, cardiovascular, oncologic, and chronic disease domains. This chapter reviews the core clinical values of X-ray, CT, and MRI, integrates recent AI-driven advances, and explores the evolving role of imaging technologies in the era of precision medicine.

title: Progress in the Application of Artificial Intelligence in Radiotherapy: From Image Guidance to Adaptive Radiation Therapy.
abstract: Radiotherapy plays a crucial role in cancer management, integral to curative approaches for 45%-50% of malignancies. However, conventional workflows face significant challenges, including operational inefficiency, inter-observer variability, and limited personalization. This review describes the evolutionary trajectory of artificial intelligence (AI) applications within the domain of radiotherapy, with a principal focus on the cardinal paradigm shift from image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) toward adaptive radiotherapy (ART). AI has demonstrably improved both the precision and efficiency of radiotherapy. This stems from its application across several critical areas: automating complex tasks in medical image analysis-like segmenting tumors, enhancing real-time motion management with the ability to capture target displacements down to the submillimeter level; and providing sophisticated decision support systems to aid clinicians. Within the sphere of ART, online adaptive systems leveraging magnetic resonance linear accelerators (MR-Linacs) and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) facilitate dynamic target delineation, dosimetric re-optimization, and cumulative dose assessment. These capabilities forge a closed-loop system based on "perception-decision-execution," effectively shifting radiotherapy beyond static planning and -toward truly personalized, dynamic treatments.

title: AI-Driven Monitoring of Biomechanical Loading in Mild Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is difficult to identify rapidly because clinical symptoms may be delayed and conventional CT or MRI often reveals no structural abnormalities. Biomechanics-based monitoring provides an objective complementary strategy by measuring head kinematics at the moment of impact and estimating the resulting brain deformation. This review summarizes how artificial intelligence (AI) can overcome two major barriers to this approach: errors in wearable-sensor measurements and the high computational cost of finite element head models. AI-based methods can denoise instrumented mouthguard signals, distinguish true impacts from false triggers, and infer impact direction, location, speed, and force. Deep learning head models can further map six-degree-of-freedom head kinematics to whole-brain strain and strain-rate distributions within milliseconds, enabling near-real-time tissue-level injury assessment. Recent advances, including kinematic feature optimization, principal component analysis, impact subtyping, transfer learning, unsupervised domain adaptation, and spatiotemporal prediction, have improved model efficiency, interpretability, and generalizability across impact scenarios. Integrating wearable sensing with AI-accelerated brain modeling could support rapid removal from exposure, earlier clinical evaluation and intervention, and monitoring of cumulative impact dose. Future research should improve sensor wearability and coupling, incorporate subject-specific brain morphology and cortical folding, represent cerebrospinal fluid mechanics more realistically, and develop unified models that jointly estimate brain deformation and predict clinically confirmed injury. AI-enabled biomechanical monitoring may therefore complement symptom- and imaging-based assessments and advance real-time, personalized mTBI detection and prevention.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Lung Diseases: Screening, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prognosis.
abstract: Pulmonary diseases currently pose significant threats to global health, spanning common chronic conditions including lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and asthma, as well as infectious and inflammatory diseases like tuberculosis, interstitial lung disease (ILD), and COVID-19. Therefore, accurate diagnosis, effective therapeutic strategies, and reliable assessment of prognosis for pulmonary diseases are essential for improving patient outcomes and safeguarding public health. Despite the increasing availability of medical imaging and pathological data owing to improvements in detection technologies, what is becoming increasingly evident are the limitations of conventional diagnosis, which relies solely on clinicians' subjective judgment based on imaging, pulmonary function, pathology, and clinical experience. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) technology, especially machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), has made significant progress in areas such as image recognition and model construction. Numerous studies have demonstrated the widespread application of AI in the screening and diagnosis of lung diseases, the optimization of treatment strategies, and prognosis assessment, revealing its remarkable ability to process and interpret complex clinical data. Although concerns persist regarding data quality, the "black box" nature of algorithms, clinical practice, and the regulatory landscape, the application of AI in lung disease research and clinical care is more and more promising. In this review, we summarize the latest advances of AI in the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary diseases, analyze the challenges and limitations of current AI technologies ranging from data and algorithms to clinical translation, and highlight directions for future research.

title: Association of Walch glenoid morphology and fracture patterns in proximal humeral fractures.
abstract: Purpose Proximal humeral fracture (PHF) assessment focuses on fracture pattern, bone quality, and patient factors, whereas glenoid morphology-central to biomechanics in glenohumeral arthritis and instability-is overlooked. We hypothesized that glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B (posterior decentring) is independently associated with complex, tuberculum-involving PHFs. Methods This single-centre, retrospective cohort study analysed 919 patients with a PHF and shoulder computed tomography (CT). Two blinded shoulder-subspecialized orthopedic trauma surgeons independently classified all cases; agreement was quantified with Cohen's κ. Fractures were classified by the Neer and AO/OTA systems and glenoid morphology by the Walch classification. The primary outcome-tuberculum involvement (Neer IV/V)-was analysed by multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age at trauma, sex, and osteoarthritis. Results The cohort comprised 919 patients (72.6% female; median age at trauma 69 years). The Walch distribution in this CT-selected cohort was type A 42.7%, B 54.4%, C 2.7%, and D 0.2%; osteoarthritis was present in 59.5%. Walch agreement was moderate (κ = 0.53), with disagreement concentrated at the A1↔B1 decentring boundary (p < 0.001). Walch type B was independently associated with tuberculum involvement (adjusted OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.56-2.74; adjusted RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.17-1.45; both p < 0.001) and with greater AO/OTA fracture complexity (adjusted ordinal OR 1.60, p < 0.001). Female sex was independently associated with the outcome (adjusted OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.05-1.97, p = 0.023); age and osteoarthritis were not significant. Conclusion In this CT-selected study population, glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B was independently associated with complex, tuberculum-involving proximal humeral fractures. The association was statistically robust but clinically modest (AUC 0.62), and Walch type B morphology represented one of several correlates of fracture pattern rather than a standalone predictor. Glenoid morphology may therefore be worth recording during CT and fracture-pattern assessment; these hypothesis-generating findings are not sufficient to modify current treatment algorithms, but support the inclusion of glenoid parameters in future risk models and prospective studies. Level of evidence Level III retrospective cohort study prognostic study.

title: Research on the morphology and injury mechanism of pilon fractures.
abstract: Introduction Understanding the relationship between injury mechanisms and fracture morphology in high-energy Pilon fractures is essential for optimizing preoperative planning and surgical outcomes. To investigate the associations between injury mechanisms and fracture morphology in high-energy Pilon fractures and to provide a theoretical basis for precision diagnosis and treatment. Methods This retrospective study included 192 patients with high-energy Pilon fractures treated at Lianyungang Second People's Hospital between January 2010 and December 2024. Using a standardized "trauma history-first plus imaging cross-validation" protocol, patients were categorized into 5 groups: dorsiflexion, varus, valgus, plantarflexion, and neutral. Two senior orthopedic surgeons (≥ 10 years of experience) independently and blindly assessed anteroposterior and lateral tibiofibular radiographs, CT scans, and three-dimensional reconstructions. Evaluated parameters included fibular fracture level and type, tibial fragment distribution, fracture angle, and Topliss classification. Interobserver reliability was assessed using Cohen's kappa coefficient. Group comparisons were performed using the chi-square (χ²) test or Fisher's exact test with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05. Results Among the 192 patients, 154 (80.2%) were male and 38 (19.8%) were female. The mean (SD) age was 43.38 (12.56) years (range, 14-71 years). Interobserver agreement was substantial for injury mechanism classification (κ = 0.82; 95% CI, 0.75-0.89) and core morphological assessments (κ = 0.87; 95% CI, 0.81-0.93). Fracture morphology differed significantly among mechanism groups (P < 0.05). Dorsiflexion injuries were characterized by the "medial + anterolateral + Die-punch" fragment pattern (45.0%; 95% CI, 23.1%-66.9%), fracture angles > 90° (65.0%), and coronal Y-shaped fractures (25.0%). Varus injuries predominantly showed the "anterolateral + posterolateral + medial + Die-punch" pattern (32.5%) and simple sagittal split fractures (40.0%). Valgus injuries were associated with comminuted fibular fractures (64.3%) and coronal V/Y-shaped tibial fractures (35.7%). Plantarflexion injuries typically involved posterolateral fragments (61.5%) and fracture angles > 90° (80.8%). Neutral injuries were characterized by complex multifragmentary comminuted fractures with Die-punch collapse (33.7%). Conclusion There is a significant and reproducible association between injury mechanisms and fracture morphology in high-energy Pilon fractures. This mechanism-based morphological characterization may provide an objective reference for preoperative assessment and individualized surgical planning. The clinical utility and prognostic value of this classification framework still need to be verified in further prospective studies with clinical outcome endpoints.

title: [Trauma-From diagnosis to intervention].
abstract: Abdominal trauma represents a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge because the large number of potentially involved organs and the complexity of the underlying injuries are difficult to capture within a standardized diagnostic approach. Both blunt and penetrating abdominal injuries can be involved as well as falls from a great height, traffic accidents or violent encounters. In addition, patients may be polytraumatized and the abdomen represents only one component of the injuries sustained but is often clinically prioritized due to the potentially immediate life-threatening nature of injuries to abdominal organs. Such injuries represent an interdisciplinary challenge and their treatment is increasingly carried out using minimally invasive procedures, often within the involvement of interventional radiology. This article aims to present both appropriate diagnostic approaches and minimally invasive treatment options.

title: [Image-guided minimally invasive treatment options for endometriosis].
abstract: Background Endometriosis affects approximately 10% of women of reproductive age with a mean diagnostic delay of 7-10 years. Image-guided procedures show increasingly promising results as minimally invasive alternatives to excision. Objective Structured overview of image-guided minimally invasive treatment options for endometriosis with focus on percutaneous cryoablation. Results Percutaneous cryoablation demonstrates the strongest evidence for extraperitoneal and intramuscular lesions and represents a valid minimally invasive alternative to excision. Three institutional cases illustrate technique and outcomes. Ethanol sclerotherapy is established for ovarian endometriomas. High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) shows promising results for abdominal wall disease; radiofrequency ablation (RFA) and microwave ablation are investigational. Conclusion Interventional radiology offers a growing therapeutic spectrum. Prospective randomized trials are needed for guideline integration.

title: Hybrid CNN-transformer model with gated feature fusion and GAN-based augmentation for MRI image classification.
abstract: Objective Brain tumor classification based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis, yet it remains challenging due to high intra-class variability, inter-class similarity, and limited annotated data. To address these challenges, this study proposes a gated hybrid convolutional neural network (CNN)-transformer architecture (GHCT-Net) that effectively integrates local and global feature representations for robust brain tumor classification in data-limited medical imaging scenarios. Methods The proposed framework combines a ConvNeXt-based convolutional branch for fine-grained spatial feature extraction with a Swin Transformer branch for modeling long-range contextual dependencies. A gate-based fusion mechanism is introduced to adaptively balance the contribution of each feature stream. Additionally, a conditional deep convolutional generative adversarial network (cDCGAN) is employed to generate class-consistent synthetic MRI samples to mitigate data scarcity. The model was evaluated on a public dataset of 7023 MRI images across four classes (glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor) under three training scenarios: original, traditionally augmented, and GAN-augmented datasets. Results The results demonstrate that the GHCT-Net achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art CNN and Transformer architectures, reaching a classification accuracy of 98.39% on the GAN-augmented dataset. Quantitative analysis, along with confusion matrices, t‑distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) visualizations, and gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) interpretability studies, confirms that the model successfully learns discriminative and clinically relevant features. Conclusion Combining a gated hybrid CNN-transformer architecture with GAN-based data augmentation provides a highly effective and robust solution for brain tumor classification, particularly in scenarios constrained by limited medical imaging data.

Objective

Brain tumor classification based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis, yet it remains challenging due to high intra-class variability, inter-class similarity, and limited annotated data. To address these challenges, this study proposes a gated hybrid convolutional neural network (CNN)-transformer architecture (GHCT-Net) that effectively integrates local and global feature representations for robust brain tumor classification in data-limited medical imaging scenarios.

Methods

The proposed framework combines a ConvNeXt-based convolutional branch for fine-grained spatial feature extraction with a Swin Transformer branch for modeling long-range contextual dependencies. A gate-based fusion mechanism is introduced to adaptively balance the contribution of each feature stream. Additionally, a conditional deep convolutional generative adversarial network (cDCGAN) is employed to generate class-consistent synthetic MRI samples to mitigate data scarcity. The model was evaluated on a public dataset of 7023 MRI images across four classes (glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor) under three training scenarios: original, traditionally augmented, and GAN-augmented datasets.

Results

The results demonstrate that the GHCT-Net achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art CNN and Transformer architectures, reaching a classification accuracy of 98.39% on the GAN-augmented dataset. Quantitative analysis, along with confusion matrices, t‑distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) visualizations, and gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) interpretability studies, confirms that the model successfully learns discriminative and clinically relevant features.

Conclusion

Combining a gated hybrid CNN-transformer architecture with GAN-based data augmentation provides a highly effective and robust solution for brain tumor classification, particularly in scenarios constrained by limited medical imaging data.

title: Associations between diabetic neuropathy and bone density and bone microarchitecture in type 2 diabetes: The Deep Phenotyping Study.
abstract: Purpose Diabetic neuropathy may contribute to skeletal fragility through sensorimotor and autonomic dysfunction. We investigated associations of peripheral and autonomic neuropathy with bone density, microarchitecture, and material properties in individuals with type 2 diabetes stratified by age. Methods In this cross-sectional study, individuals with type 2 diabetes with (n = 50, mean age 67.4 years) and without (n = 73, mean age 62.2 years) diabetic neuropathy underwent assessment of bone structure and quality using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry with trabecular bone score, high-resolution peripheral computed tomography, and microindentation, alongside evaluation of neuropathy and autonomic function. Associations were assessed using multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and BMI, with age-stratified analyses ( < 65 and ≥65 years). Results In individuals < 65 years, neuropathy was associated with markedly lower areal bone mineral density at the total hip (β =-0.15 g/cm 2 , 95% CI -0.24 to-0.06), and femoral neck (β =-0.18 g/cm², -0.26 to -0.09), and with lower TBS (β =-1.56, -2.23 to -0.89). At the tibia, neuropathy was associated with lower total, cortical and trabecular volumetric bone mineral density, lower trabecular bone volume fraction, and higher cortical porosity. At the radius, lower cortical volumetric bone mineral density and lower trabecular number were observed. No significant associations were observed for Bone Material Strength index or in individuals ≥ 65 years. Conclusion In individuals with type 2 diabetes <65 years, diabetic neuropathy is associated with lower bone density and differences in cortical and trabecular microarchitecture. These findings suggest neuropathy may be associated with impaired bone quality in younger adults with type 2 diabetes.

title: Interpreting liver volume changes after rifampicin in healthy volunteers.
abstract: Rifampicin-associated liver volume changes in healthy volunteers provide an opportunity to examine the human relevance of xenobiotic-induced liver growth. This Comment considers three aspects of the clinical analysis relevant to interpreting the observed response. Clarification of whether the volumetric outcomes and choice of normalisation were prespecified, alongside paired treatment effects and confidence intervals, would help establish the basis for inference and assess the response's magnitude and precision. For a small volumetric response, blinded repeat segmentation of existing magnetic resonance images and details of scan timing and pre-scan intake would help assess reproducibility under comparable physiological conditions. Associations between 4β-hydroxycholesterol and liver volume could also be examined using within-participant rifampicin-minus-placebo differences, with appropriate attention to the crossover design and an exploratory interpretation. Most of these suggestions could be addressed through protocol information and existing imaging and crossover data, strengthening interpretation of the human findings and guiding further investigation of pregnane X receptor-mediated liver growth.

title: IMPROving MYelin imaging in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (IMPROMYMS study): protocol for a prospective longitudinal study.
abstract: Introduction It is increasingly recognized that patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) may experience disability progression in the absence of clinical relapses and new lesions, a phenomenon known as progression independent of relapse- and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) activity (PIRMA). The biological basis of this type of progression remains poorly understood. Demyelination is the central pathological hallmark of RRMS. Conventional clinical MRI protocols focus primarily on detecting focal lesions. However, advanced imaging techniques that quantify myelin content can provide additional insights beyond visible lesions, helping to better understand the mechanisms that drive clinical deterioration. Objective Therefore, this study named IMPROving MYelin imaging in patients with relapsing-remitting Multiple Sclerosis (IMPROMYMS study) aims to apply myelin imaging techniques to study clinically defined disease progression in patients with RRMS, by assessing myelin content and comparing it to patients with RRMS without progression of the disease. Methods In total, 97 patients with RRMS will be included and followed for 2.5 years. Participants will undergo MRI scanning at baseline and after 2 years and have regular clinical follow-up visits. Besides conventional MRI, advanced imaging sequences will be scanned, including gradient spin echo (GRASE), multi-echo gradient echo (ME-GRE), diffusion and functional MRI. Additionally, blood samples will be collected longitudinally to assess circulating biomarkers of neuroaxonal damage and astrocytic activation. Participants can also use the smartphone symptom-monitoring app MS Sherpa to enable more frequent monitoring of functional changes in daily life. In addition, 30 healthy controls will be scanned once as a reference group. In this study, we expect to find radiological prognostic markers of an increased risk of developing PIRMA, so that disease management strategies can be altered accordingly.

title: Tumor-masked structural connectomics for assessing tract-specific white matter disruption associated with glioma aggressiveness: an interpretable machine learning pilot study.
abstract: Purpose To assess the feasibility of personalized tumor-masked structural connectomics combined with interpretable machine learning (ML) for differentiating low-grade gliomas (LGG) from high-grade gliomas (HGG), and to identify candidate tract-specific connectomic biomarkers of glioma aggressiveness. Methods Thirty-five patients with histopathologically confirmed gliomas (20 LGG, 15 HGG) underwent preoperative diffusion tensor imaging and T1-weighted MRI. Tumor-masked probabilistic tractography was used to reconstruct individualized structural connectomes based on 50 white matter (WM) tract labels. We evaluated 296 graph-theoretical features using sequential feature selection and Random Forest classification within a strictly isolated nested cross-validation framework. We used SHAP analysis for model interpretation. Sensitivity analyses compared clinical-radiological, connectomic, and combined feature sets. Results The leak-free pure connectomics model achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.814 ± 0.327 (95% CI, 0.500-1.000), with a macro-F1 score of 0.786 ± 0.265. Restricting the analysis to non-zero connectomic features yielded a mean AUC of 0.833 ± 0.167. The clinical-radiological model achieved a mean AUC of 0.817 ± 0.149, while the combined clinical-radiological and connectomic model showed the highest point estimate (AUC, 0.933 ± 0.109; 95% CI, 0.798-1.068). SHAP analysis highlighted the sagittal stratum, medial lemniscus, and superior fronto-occipital fasciculus among the most informative WM pathways. Conclusion Tumor-masked structural connectomics combined with interpretable ML demonstrated preliminary feasibility for identifying candidate imaging biomarkers associated with glioma aggressiveness in neuroradiological practice. These findings are exploratory and represent internal estimates from a single cohort; external validation in independent, multi-center cohorts is required before any potential clinical application.

title: MRI Radiomics and Deep Learning for Differentiating Spinal Tuberculosis from Spinal Metastasis: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Objectives To develop radiomics model, 2D deep learning (2D DL) model, 2.5D deep learning (2.5D DL) model, 3D deep learning (3D DL) model, and their fusion models to differentiate spinal tuberculosis (STB) from spinal metastasis (SM) based on MR imaging. Methods This retrospective study included 186 STB patients and 219 SM patients. Patients from three hospitals were divided into a training set (n = 191), an internal test set (n = 82) and an external test set (n = 132). Using the ResNet50 network pre-trained leveraging the ImageNet dataset, we developed 2D, 2.5D, and 3D deep learning models based on MR imaging. We constructed the radiomics model by using PyRadiomics to extract radiomics features. Deep learning models and radiomics model were used to construct two fusion models: the feature-based model (Rad_DL_FB) and the decision-based model (Rad_DL_DB). And the accuracy of these models was validated. Results In the internal test set, the Rad_DL_FB model demonstrated superior performance compared to other models, achieving the highest AUC of 0.971 (95% CI: 0.953-0.989) and accuracy of 0.927. In the external test set, the Rad_DL_DB model demonstrated superior performance compared to other models, achieving the highest AUC of 0.961 (95% CI: 0.940-0.982) and accuracy of 0.909. Furthermore, fusion-model assistance significantly improved the diagnostic accuracy of junior spine surgeons and narrowed the observed performance gap between junior and senior surgeons. Conclusion The fusion models including Rad_DL_FB model and Rad_DL_DB model, which integrates radiomics features and deep learning features of different dimensions, can effectively differentiate STB from SM, thereby assisting clinicians in making clinical decisions.

title: CT-based bone mineral density estimation using HU, radiomics, and deep learning.
abstract: Purpose To develop and test models that estimate bone mineral density (BMD) from thoracolumbar junction CT images using Hounsfield unit (HU) assessment, radiomics, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Methods We retrospectively identified patients who underwent lumbar dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry and CT covering T12 and L1 within 6 months at four hospitals between 2014 and 2025. In total, 465 patients were eligible for T12 analysis, and 448 for L1. Data from two institutions were used for training/validation and data from the other two for external testing. We developed five models: region-of-interest-based HU regression; volume-of-interest (VOI)-based HU regression; radiomics; CNN; and an ensemble combining VOI, radiomics, and CNN. Performance was assessed using mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R 2 ), and Bland-Altman limits of agreement (LoA). Results For T12, the CNN model performed best among the single models (MAE: 0.122, RMSE: 0.157, R 2 : 0.603), whereas the ensemble model showed a slightly higher MAE (0.128) but lower RMSE (0.154) and higher R 2 (0.620). For L1, the radiomics model was the best single model (MAE: 0.124, RMSE: 0.155, R 2 : 0.582), while the ensemble showed numerically improved performance (MAE: 0.116, RMSE: 0.145, R 2 : 0.633). Pairwise comparisons showed no significant difference in absolute prediction errors between the ensemble and the best single model at either T12 or L1. Conclusion We developed an ensemble framework integrating volumetric HU assessment, radiomics, and CNNs to estimate BMD from thoracolumbar junction CT images. External testing across two independent institutions demonstrated promising performance for BMD estimation.

title: Prognostic value of dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI and plasma angiogenic markers for survival outcomes in HPV-negative oropharyngeal carcinoma treated with concurrent chemoradiotherapy.
abstract: Purpose Dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) enables non-invasive assessment of tumour vascularity, while circulating angiogenic factors may reflect tumour-associated angiogenic activity. We investigated whether DCE-MRI perfusion parameters and plasma angiogenic factors measured before and early during concurrent chemoradiotherapy (cCRT) are associated with survival in human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC). Methods In this prospective single-centre study, 24 patients with locally advanced HPV-negative OPSCC treated with cCRT were analysed. DCE-MRI perfusion parameters (Ktrans, Kep, Ve, iAUC) were analysed at baseline and early intra-treatment (20 Gy), while plasma angiogenic factors (vascular endothelial growth factor [VEGF], connective tissue growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor-AB, angiogenin, endostatin, and thrombospondin-1) were analysed at baseline, early intra-treatment and post-treatment (10-12 weeks). Disease-specific survival (DSS) was assessed using univariable Cox regression (hazard ratios [HRs] per 1-SD) and Kaplan-Meier analysis with false-discovery-rate correction. Results Seven patients died of the index cancer. Higher baseline Ktrans (HR per 1-SD 0.30, p = 0.031) and higher early intra-treatment plasma VEGF (HR 0.37, p = 0.043) were nominally associated with better DSS; VEGF also showed separation in Kaplan-Meier analysis (3-year DSS 92% vs. 36%, log-rank p = 0.016). Effect estimates were similar after exploratory adjustment for tumour volume but attenuated after adjustment for stage. No association remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction, and the early VEGF association partly overlapped with local treatment response. Conclusion In this exploratory analysis, baseline DCE-MRI perfusion (Ktrans) and plasma VEGF showed hypothesis-generating associations with DSS in HPV-negative OPSCC. As no association survived multiplicity correction, these findings require validation in larger independent cohorts.

title: Pediatric Bow Hunter syndrome: clinical, vascular, and longitudinal findings from a single center and systematic review of the literature.
abstract: Purpose Bow Hunter syndrome (BHS) is a rare cause of pediatric vertebral artery dissection (VAD) and posterior circulation arterial ischemic stroke (AIS) due to dynamic compression during head rotation. Imaging features, vascular evolution, and outcomes remain poorly defined. Methods We reviewed children with definite or probable BHS diagnosed at a tertiary pediatric center between 2010 and 2026. A systematic review identified published pediatric cases (0-18 years) of definite/probable BHS. Results Twelve boys were included (mean age, 7.3 years; mean follow-up, 54.4 months). Posterior circulation AIS occurred in 10/12 (83.3%), with multifocal infarcts of different ages in eight and additional anterior circulation embolic infarcts in three. VAD was bilateral in 6/12 (50%), consistently involving V3. Distal posterior cerebral and/or superior cerebellar artery stenosis or occlusion with collateral networks occurred in 7/12 (58.3%); basilar artery involvement in 4/12. Dynamic vascular imaging demonstrated position-dependent vertebral artery compromise in 9/12 patients (eight by rotational DSA and one by Doppler ultrasound). Craniocervical junction variants were present in 10/12 (83.3%), without flexion-extension instability. Early recurrent AIS occurred in 5/10 despite antithrombotic therapy. Serial imaging showed early vascular evolution followed by stabilization. Two patients underwent surgery; the others were treated conservatively. Conclusions A rotational mechanical mechanism should be considered in children with posterior circulation AIS and V3 abnormalities, particularly when preceded by overlooked prodromal symptoms or minor trauma- and sport-related triggers. Multimodal neurovascular imaging, especially dynamic angiography, is essential for diagnosis, surveillance, and individualized treatment planning aimed at preventing further vascular injury.

title: Longitudinal quantitative MRI feature analysis in paediatric focal cortical dysplasia: a retrospective longitudinal cohort study.
abstract: Purpose Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a common cause of treatment-resistant epilepsy and can be difficult to detect on MRI. Although traditionally considered static, lesion visibility may vary across scans. We assessed whether MELD-derived lesional imaging features differ across serial MRI in histologically confirmed paediatric FCD type II. Methods Twenty-one patients with histopathologically confirmed FCD type II underwent paired T1-weighted MRI; 13 also had paired FLAIR imaging. Images were processed using FastSurfer and a modified MELD feature-extraction pipeline. Lesion-mask feature values were compared with anatomically matched contralateral regions, and time-corrected longitudinal lesion-contralateral differences were calculated. Blinded qualitative neuroradiological review was available for 20/21 subjects. Results FCD lesions demonstrated quantitative feature differences from contralateral cortex. In the FLAIR cohort, longitudinal lesion-contralateral differences were consistently positive across sampled grey and white matter depths and remained significant after false discovery rate correction (mean paired differences 0.607-0.737; all pFDR = 0.009). Protocol-restricted FLAIR sensitivity analyses preserved the direction of effect, although restricted subgroups were underpowered. In T1-weighted MRI, longitudinal lesion-contralateral differences were positive across grey matter intensity features, greatest at 75% cortical thickness (mean paired difference 0.185, 95% CI 0.060-0.309, p = 0.006), but no T1 feature survived false discovery rate correction. Neuroradiological review identified possible visually appreciable interval change in a minority of cases, with most apparent change attributed to acquisition-related variation or artefact. Conclusion Quantitative MRI-derived FCD features can vary across serial paediatric MRI. These findings demonstrate longitudinal imaging feature variability, most consistently in FLAIR-derived measures, with implications for repeat imaging and machine learning derived lesion detection.
