title: Impact of preoperative skeletal muscle mass and body mass index on the prognosis of patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Objectives Skeletal muscle mass (SMM) and nutritional status influence cancer prognosis. Cancer-related systemic inflammation may drive muscle atrophy and loss of SMM. In this retrospective study, we evaluated the prognostic impact of preoperative SMM and body mass index (BMI) in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). Materials and methods Overall, 150 patients with OSCC (excluding carcinoma in situ) who underwent curative surgery at our department between 2010 and 2019 were included. SMM was quantified by the sternocleidomastoid muscle cross-sectional area at the third cervical vertebra (C3), using sex-specific cutoff values. BMI was categorized as underweight (<18.5), normal (18.5-<25), or obese (≥25). General condition was evaluated using the Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI) and HALP score (Hemoglobin, Albumin, Lymphocyte, and Platelet), and their associations with overall survival (OS) were analyzed. Results Overall, 32.6% of patients had low SMM. SMM was significantly correlated with BMI, GNRI, and HALP. SMM, reconstruction (present/absent), and a combined index of SMM and BMI were significantly associated with OS. Patients with low SMM and high BMI showed poorer survival. However, this subgroup comprised only five patients, and this finding should therefore be interpreted with caution. In univariable analysis, clinical stage, reconstruction, and SMM were significantly associated with OS. In multivariable analysis, SMM remained an independent prognostic factor. Conclusions Preoperative low SMM was independently associated with poorer OS in patients with OSCC and may provide additional prognostic information when assessed alongside BMI. Clinical relevance Preoperative assessment of SMM using routine computed tomography may improve risk stratification in patients with OSCC and help identify low SMM that may not be apparent from BMI alone.

title: Treatment strategies for primary intraosseous squamous cell carcinoma of the solid type in the mandible: a single-centre retrospective analysis.
abstract: Purpose Primary intraosseous squamous cell carcinoma (PIOSCC) of the mandible is a rare malignancy, and evidence regarding optimal management remains limited. This retrospective study aimed to evaluate clinical outcomes, explore potential clinicopathological associations, and assess the diagnostic performance of imaging modalities in patients with solid-type PIOSCC treated at a single centre. Methods Fifteen consecutive patients with solid-type PIOSCC of the mandible were retrospectively reviewed. Clinical variables, including peri-mandibular muscle infiltration and surgical margin status, imaging findings from computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance (MR) imaging, and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT), treatment modalities, and survival outcomes were analysed. Overall and disease-specific survival were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Results The 5-year disease-specific survival rate was 72.2%. For contextual reference, the corresponding 5-year disease-specific survival rate in surgically treated lower gingival squamous cell carcinoma during the same period was 75.5%. Infiltration of the peri-mandibular muscle, combined with close surgical margins, may be associated with poorer clinical outcomes. Among the various imaging modalities, fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) showed the strongest correlation with the pathological maximum tumour diameter in this exploratory analysis. Conclusions This retrospective single-centre analysis suggests that peri-mandibular muscle infiltration and surgical margin status may be associated with prognosis in patients with solid-type PIOSCC of the mandible. FDG-PET may provide complementary information for tumour assessment. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Rare parotid gland metastasis from colorectal cancer: a case report and review of the literature.
abstract: Metastasis of colorectal carcinoma (CRC) to the parotid gland is exceptionally rare, with only a few cases reported in the literature. We describe a 70 year old woman previously treated for sigmoid adenocarcinoma who developed a painful right parotid mass three years after hemicolectomy and adjuvant XELOX chemotherapy. Fine needle aspiration confirmed metastatic sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma through characteristic immunohistochemical markers, including CDX 2 and Villin positivity. A review of the 8 reported cases (including the current one) shows the disease occurs in patients at a mean age of 63 years (range, 34 to 83). There is no gender or side predilection. The overall features indicate that parotid metastasis from CRC typically occurs with widespread disease and carries a poor prognosis. Diagnosis is challenging because parotid metastases often mimic primary salivary gland tumours clinically and radiologically, making immunohistochemistry essential for distinguishing intestinal adenocarcinoma from primary salivary malignancies. Reported outcomes remain poor, reflecting advanced systemic disease at presentation. This case emphasises the need to consider metastatic CRC in the differential diagnosis of new parotid masses in patients with a history of colorectal malignancy. Early recognition, accurate diagnosis through imaging and histopathology, and multidisciplinary management are crucial. This case highlights the importance of considering metastatic CRC in the differential diagnosis of parotid masses in patients with a known primary malignancy.

title: Ultrasound screening and secukinumab intervention for subclinical and clinical psoriatic arthritis: a prospective real-world study.
abstract: Background This prospective real-world study primarily evaluated clinical and ultrasonographic outcomes after 24 weeks of secukinumab treatment in participants with subclinical or clinical psoriatic arthritis (PsA) identified through a risk-based musculoskeletal ultrasound screening pathway. A secondary descriptive objective was to characterize the screening pathway and the identification of ultrasound-detected subclinical PsA. Methods Participants with psoriasis were enrolled at the Department of Dermatology, Tianjin Medical University, from September 1, 2022, to December 31, 2023. Participants considered at increased risk of PsA underwent musculoskeletal ultrasound assessment. They were classified as having subclinical PsA, clinical PsA, or no qualifying inflammatory ultrasound findings according to clinical and imaging findings. Participants who initiated secukinumab and completed 24 weeks of treatment and follow-up were included in the therapeutic outcome analysis. The primary outcome was the proportion achieving PASI100 at week 24. Secondary outcomes included PASI75/90 responses, ACR20/50/70 responses in clinical PsA, ultrasound changes, quality-of-life measures, and adverse events. Results Of 358 enrolled participants, 249 (69.6%) were classified as being at high risk of PsA based on the PEST score and/or prespecified clinical risk features. Among 194 high-risk participants who underwent musculoskeletal ultrasound screening, 159 had qualifying inflammatory ultrasound findings, leading to diagnoses of 42 with subclinical PsA and 117 with clinical PsA. A total of 38 participants completed a 24-week course of secukinumab. At week 24, 87.5% of subclinical PsA participants and 95.45% of clinical PsA participants achieved complete skin clearance (Psoriasis Area and Severity Index, PASI100). In the clinical PsA group, American College of Rheumatology (ACR) 20/50/70 response rates were 95.45%, 86.36%, and 72.73%, respectively. Ultrasound findings of synovitis and enthesitis improved descriptively in both groups. No serious adverse events were reported among the 38 treatment completers. Conclusion In this exploratory, single-arm real-world cohort, a risk-based musculoskeletal ultrasound pathway identified participants with imaging positive for inflammatory synovio-entheseal involvement compatible with subclinical or clinical PsA. Among the small group who completed 24 weeks of secukinumab, substantial descriptive improvements in skin outcomes, clinical measures, and selected inflammatory ultrasound findings were observed. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound or demonstrate that secukinumab prevents progression from subclinical to clinical PsA. Key Points • In this exploratory cohort, a risk-based musculoskeletal ultrasound pathway identified imaging inflammatory abnormalities compatible with subclinical PsA in selected high-risk participants with psoriasis; the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound was not assessed. • Among 38 treatment completers who received secukinumab for dermatologic indications, high PASI75/90/100 and ACR20/50/70 response rates were observed at 24 weeks; given the single-arm, uncontrolled design, these responses cannot be attributed specifically to secukinumab. • Inflammatory ultrasound findings of synovitis and enthesitis improved descriptively in both groups, supporting ultrasound as a complementary tool for monitoring treatment response rather than as a stand-alone diagnostic tes. • Enthesitis most frequently involved the finger flexor and extensor tendons, the quadriceps tendon, and the Achilles tendon; isolated structural entheseal abnormalities (e.g., bone spurs and calcifications) were common and were not interpreted as active inflammation.

title: Isolated body lateropulsion due to a paramedian mesencephalic stroke.
abstract: We report a 71-year-old man who presented with acute recurrent falls due to isolated body lateropulsion to the right, as sole neurological deficit. Brain MRI revealed a left paramedian mesencephalic infarction involving the interstitial nucleus of Cajal (INC) and medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). Isolated body lateropulsion is a rare clinical presentation produced by lesions affecting the graviceptive pathway, which processes gravitational input and body orientation relative to vertical in order to maintain upright posture and spatial orientation. Although internuclear ophtalmoplegia or abnormalities of vertical or torsional eye position have been associated with lesions of the INC and MLF, these were absent in our patient.The patient recovered fully within three months, consistent with the favorable prognosis of isolated lateropulsion due to stroke. This case highlights an under-recognized topodiagnostic pattern within the graviceptive pathway.

title: Navigated laser photocoagulation reduces injection burden and recurrence in diabetic macular edema: A 24-month real-world comparative study.
abstract: Diabetic macular edema (DME) requires frequent intravitreal anti-VEGF injections, creating substantial treatment burden. Navigated laser photocoagulation offers precise microaneurysm targeting, but its adjunctive benefit with anti-VEGF therapy remains inadequately documented in real-world settings. This retrospective comparative study included 87 treatment-naive DME patients followed for 24 months. Group A (n = 42) received intravitreal bevacizumab monotherapy; Group B (n = 45) received combination therapy (bevacizumab plus Navilas navigated laser photocoagulation). Primary endpoints were injection burden, recurrence rates, and hyperreflective dot (HRD) count as an inflammatory biomarker on spectral-domain optical coherence tomography. Combination therapy required significantly fewer injections over 24 months (4.6 ± 1.8 vs. 7.3 ± 2.1; p < 0.001), representing 37% reduction. Recurrence rates were lower in the combination group (17.8% vs. 33.3%; p = 0.03). title: Endoscopic NIRAF-LSCI multimodal system with pseudo-color visualization for parathyroid autofluorescence localization and tissue perfusion assessment: preclinical validation.
abstract: Postoperative hypoparathyroidism remains a prevalent complication of thyroid surgery, primarily caused by unrecognized parathyroid gland (PG) injury or devascularization. While near-infrared autofluorescence (NIRAF) enables accurate PG localization, it provides no functional perfusion information; conversely, laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI) offers label-free real-time perfusion assessment. Herein, we validated a multimodal endoscopic system integrating NIRAF and LSCI for simultaneous PG identification and vascular evaluation, focusing on LSCI perfusion performance and the clinical practicability of its pseudo-color semi-quantitative visualization. The system was tested in 8 Sprague-Dawley rats, where rat thyroids with homologous blood supply served as perfusion surrogates due to the minute volume of rat PGs. Imaging was performed under three strictly controlled in situ conditions: intact native vascularization, partial vascular occlusion, and complete vascular occlusion. LSCI pseudo-color visualization was generated via a standardized pipeline including temporal laser speckle contrast analysis (tLASCA)-based blood flow index (BFI) calculation, baseline-anchored joint 5th-95th percentile normalization, and Jet colormap mapping. Intraoperative probe-based quantitative NIRAF was used to validate NIRAF-visual signal foci. NIRAF clearly identified PGs with a fluorescence intensity of 149.8 ± 8.7 mV, significantly higher than thyroid (93.8 ± 8.0 mV), trachea (84.6 ± 9.1 mV), and muscle (66.3 ± 10.4 mV) (all P < 0.001), achieving 100% positive predictive value (PPV) and 100% negative predictive value (NPV), with zero false-positive findings among all NIRAF-visual foci. PPV was determined using both probe-based NIRAF and histopathology as dual validation references, whereas NPV was determined using postoperative histopathology alone as the reference standard. LSCI speckle contrast increased progressively with decreasing perfusion, with speckle contrast values mapped to a continuous blue-to-red real-time pseudo-color perfusion visualization. Histopathology confirmed all fluorescent tissues as PGs. This multimodal system targets two core clinical needs for intraoperative PG protection, and its standardized pseudo-color semi-quantitative workflow provides real-time label-free perfusion visualization. It shows potential to serve as an intraoperative adjunct to guide parathyroid preservation decisions and reduce reliance on delayed hormonal test results.

title: Standard anterior temporal lobectomy using a retractorless technique in patients with drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy: long-term seizure outcomes and predictors of postoperative seizure freedom.
abstract: Background Fixed brain retractors risk focal ischemia and cortical injury. Although retractorless dynamic retraction is established in skull base surgery, its role in epilepsy surgery remains poorly characterized. Objective To evaluate long-term seizure outcomes, safety, and reliability of retractorless standard anterior temporal lobectomy (ATL) in drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE), and identify predictors of seizure freedom. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 42 patients who underwent retractorless standard ATL for drug-resistant MTLE. Dynamic retraction used bipolar forceps and pressure-controlled suction. The primary outcome was seizure freedom (Engel Class Ia) at minimum 24-month follow-up; secondary outcomes were complications and resection adequacy on postoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Predictors were identified using multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models. Results At a mean follow-up of 66.3 months, 69% of patients achieved complete seizure freedom (Engel Class Ia), and 83.3% achieved freedom from disabling seizures (Engel Class I). Postoperative MRI confirmed adequate resection in 95.2% of cases. Complications were uncommon and unrelated to retraction injury. Low preoperative seizure frequency (< 3 seizures/week) was the sole independent predictor of seizure freedom (odds ratio, 24.21; P = 0.026), while higher frequency (≥ 3 seizures/week) was associated with increased recurrence risk (hazard ratio, 7.34; P = 0.042). Conclusion Retractorless standard ATL is safe and effective for drug-resistant MTLE, achieving long-term seizure control while minimizing retraction-associated risks. Preoperative seizure burden was the dominant prognostic marker, supporting early surgical intervention.

title: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to posterior third ventricle pathology: One or two burr hole approaches for ETV and biopsy.
abstract: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) and tumor biopsy is a frequent procedure for third ventricular tumors. While some authors favor one approach to achieve both goals, others support the selection of two approaches to avoid fornical damage and venous hemorrhage. Here the authors present their experience with both techniques. A retrospective analysis was conducted on cases which underwent an ETV and a tumor procedure in lesions of the posterior third ventricle from 2011 to 2025. Patient records, pre- and postoperative imaging and intraoperative video recordings were retrospectively analyzed. Twenty-six patients met the inclusion criteria: 13 were treated with one, the other 13 with two approaches. The surgical goal of ETV and tumor biopsy/resection was achieved in all cases. No procedure was abandoned. No postoperative complication was observed. Intraoperative forniceal injury was observed in 8/26 patients (31%). Intraoperative bleeding was found in 81% (21/26 cases). In 19% of cases (5/26 cases), intraoperative bleeding required a longer irrigation time but no switch to dry field technique or open surgery was needed. On follow up, three patients required ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement. Thus, ETV success scored 88.5% (23/26 cases). On 2D MRI, the mean intertrajectory angle was smaller in the one-burr-hole group than in the two-burr-hole group (41.8° ± 3.5° vs. 48.7° ± 5.4°; p = 0.001). Lesions of the posterior third ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus are ideal candidates for an endoscopic approach. The overall success rate is very high with acceptable surgical risks. In this cohort, larger intertrajectory angles were associated with selection of a two-burr-hole approach. The approximate 45° value was derived post hoc and requires external validation.

title: Deep learning MGMT promoter methylation status prediction in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma using multiparametric MRI: Benchmark vs. real‑world performance.
abstract: Preoperative determination of O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter methylation status is of major prognostic and predictive relevance in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, yet currently depends on invasive tissue sampling. This study investigates deep learning-based strategies for MGMT prediction from multiparametric MRIs, with particular emphasis on robustness and generalizability under heterogeneous, multicenter conditions. A total of 949 glioblastoma cases were analyzed, integrating public benchmark data from the Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge (BraTS) with multi-institutional private cohorts acquired across diverse scanners and imaging protocols. Four complementary experimental settings were designed to compare reproduced literature baselines, private-only training, whole-brain end-to-end models, and segmentation-guided region-of-interest (ROI) pipelines. Tumor delineation was performed using an nnU-Net framework with expert quality control, and multiple three-dimensional convolutional neural network architectures were evaluated. Model performance was highest on the homogeneous BraTS benchmark, where a whole-brain DenseNet121 achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.80. However, marked performance deterioration was observed when models were evaluated on independent held-out multicenter test set. In contrast, segmentation-guided ROI-based approaches showed a more stable performance profile in this preliminary independent held-out multicenter test. Explicit lesion localization was associated with reduction in false-positive classifications, suggesting a potential benefit for performance stability across heterogeneous datasets, although validation in external cohorts from institutions not represented during training is required. Collectively, these results demonstrate that upstream methodological choices, especially tumor segmentation and ROI definition, remain critical determinants of performance in MRI-based radiogenomic modeling. Future studies should emphasize prospective multicenter validation, domain-shift harmonization, multimodal data integration, and uncertainty-aware deep learning to enhance robustness and interpretability.

title: Endovascular robotic-assisted system for cerebral angiography (ERASE): Rationale, design, and protocol of a multicenter randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Neurointerventional therapy is a cornerstone in managing head and neck vascular disorders, with cerebral angiography serving as its fundamental diagnostic and therapeutic backbone. However, manual cerebral angiography is associated with several inherent limitations. While existing robotic-assisted systems have shown promise in mitigating some of these issues, they face challenges such as limited compatibility, lengthy setup times, and a lack of high-quality real-world evidence. The ERASE trial is a multicenter, prospective, randomized controlled trial (RCT). A total of 660 eligible patients will be enrolled from seven comprehensive stroke centers in China and randomized 1:1 to either the robotic-assisted group or the control group. Both groups use the Seldinger technique for femoral/radial artery access. Operators undergo standardized training on the robotic system. The trial adopts a prospective randomized open-label blinded endpoint (PROBE) design, with all imaging endpoints adjudicated via blinded review by an independent imaging core laboratory. All patients are followed up at baseline, end of surgery, 24 h postoperatively, and 7 days post-discharge. The primary efficacy outcome is the clinical success rate. The primary safety outcome is the incidence of perioperative/postoperative complications (e.g., vascular perforation, dissection, pseudoaneurysm), serious adverse events, and device malfunctions. Secondary outcomes include technical failure rate, overall procedural time, pre-puncture setup time, mean catheterization time per target vessel, super-selective technique success rate, DSA fluoroscopy time, participant radiation dose, primary operator radiation dose, contrast agent volume and instrument performance evaluation. A key safety endpoint is the rate of new asymptomatic cerebral infarctions detected via postoperative brain MRI-diffusion-weighted imaging. As the RCT focusing on the YDHB-NS01 Ver 2.0 system, the ERASE trial addresses critical unmet needs in neurointerventional practice and will generate high-quality evidence for robotic-assisted cerebral angiography. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07182188. TRIAL REGISTRATION DATE: 2025-09-18.
originalAbstract: Neurointerventional therapy is a cornerstone in managing head and neck vascular disorders, with cerebral angiography serving as its fundamental diagnostic and therapeutic backbone. However, manual cerebral angiography is associated with several inherent limitations. While existing robotic-assisted systems have shown promise in mitigating some of these issues, they face challenges such as limited compatibility, lengthy setup times, and a lack of high-quality real-world evidence. The ERASE trial is a multicenter, prospective, randomized controlled trial (RCT). A total of 660 eligible patients will be enrolled from seven comprehensive stroke centers in China and randomized 1:1 to either the robotic-assisted group or the control group. Both groups use the Seldinger technique for femoral/radial artery access. Operators undergo standardized training on the robotic system. The trial adopts a prospective randomized open-label blinded endpoint (PROBE) design, with all imaging endpoints adjudicated via blinded review by an independent imaging core laboratory. All patients are followed up at baseline, end of surgery, 24 h postoperatively, and 7 days post-discharge. The primary efficacy outcome is the clinical success rate. The primary safety outcome is the incidence of perioperative/postoperative complications (e.g., vascular perforation, dissection, pseudoaneurysm), serious adverse events, and device malfunctions. Secondary outcomes include technical failure rate, overall procedural time, pre-puncture setup time, mean catheterization time per target vessel, super-selective technique success rate, DSA fluoroscopy time, participant radiation dose, primary operator radiation dose, contrast agent volume and instrument performance evaluation. A key safety endpoint is the rate of new asymptomatic cerebral infarctions detected via postoperative brain MRI-diffusion-weighted imaging. As the RCT focusing on the YDHB-NS01 Ver 2.0 system, the ERASE trial addresses critical unmet needs in neurointerventional practice and will generate high-quality evidence for robotic-assisted cerebral angiography. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07182188. TRIAL REGISTRATION DATE: 2025-09-18.

title: Intraoperative technology in skull base and vascular neurosurgery: a two-stage cross-sectional national survey.
abstract: Skull base and vascular neurosurgery rely on diverse intraoperative technologies, but contemporary data describing how frequently they are used at the level of individual operations are limited. On behalf of the Society of British Neurological Surgeons (SBNS) MedTech Committee, we aimed to establish a dated descriptive baseline of reported technology use across three operative paradigms. We conducted a two-stage cross-sectional survey of neurosurgeons in the UK and Ireland via the Society of British Neurological Surgeons (SBNS). Six MedTech Committee members compiled a pragmatic technology list. Respondents reported frequency of use for three exemplar procedures: transsphenoidal pituitary adenoma, retrosigmoid vestibular schwannoma, and pterional aneurysm surgery. Use was recorded on a four-point ordinal scale and analysed descriptively, with Kendall's tau-b used to explore the relationship between experience and reported use. Twenty-four responses from 20 of the 32 adult or mixed adult-paediatric UK units were analysed (11 units per index procedure). Reported use was strongly procedure specific. Neuronavigation was used always or almost always by 8/12 transsphenoidal respondents but infrequently elsewhere. Endoscopy had displaced microscopy in transsphenoidal surgery, whereas microscopy was used always or almost always by all retrosigmoid and pterional respondents. Indocyanine green and micro-Doppler were routine for aneurysms. Neurophysiological monitoring was universal for vestibular schwannoma but evenly divided for aneurysms. Exoscopes, intraoperative MRI and robotics were used infrequently or not at all; augmented reality was reported by 5/13 pterional respondents. No association was found between experience and reported use, though this was underpowered. Reported intraoperative technology use is strongly shaped by operative paradigm, with established technologies clustering around recurring procedural needs. Newer technologies were used infrequently. Because availability was not recorded, non-use cannot be distinguished from lack of access. These data provide a dated baseline against which future change can be assessed.

title: Prognostic impact of concurrent radiographic progression at PSA-defined transition to castration resistance in de novo metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer.
abstract: Background Radiographic progression (rPD) at castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) diagnosis remains poorly characterized in real-world settings. We assessed its prognostic impact and the clinical features of patients with rPD in real-world de novo metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC). Methods We retrospectively analyzed 280 patients with de novo mCSPC who progressed to prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-defined CRPC from two multi-institutional cohorts: a conventional androgen deprivation therapy or combined androgen blockade (ADT/CAB) cohort (n = 223) and an upfront intensification cohort (n = 57). At CRPC diagnosis, patients were categorized as having PSA-only progression or PSA + rPD. Post-CRPC overall survival (OS) was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards models, while rPD-associated characteristics were examined using logistic regression. Results Patients with PSA + rPD had significantly shorter post-CRPC OS than those with PSA-only progression (ADT/CAB: 22 vs. 47 months, P < 0.001; upfront: 14 vs. 24 months, P = 0.010). Univariate Cox regression confirmed the adverse prognostic impact of rPD (hazard ratios, 2.11 [95% CI 1.39-3.21] and 2.43 [95% CI 1.20-4.96]). Lower baseline PSA levels were associated with rPD in both the ADT/CAB (odds ratio [OR], 0.65; 95% CI 0.42-0.99; P = 0.046) and upfront (OR, 0.29; 95% CI 0.12-0.71; P = 0.006) cohorts. Conclusion Radiographic progression at CRPC diagnosis predicts poor post-CRPC survival in real-world de novo mCSPC patients, regardless of initial treatment. Lower baseline PSA may be associated with rPD, although this exploratory finding requires validation. These findings support considering radiographic evaluation at CRPC diagnosis.

Background

Radiographic progression (rPD) at castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) diagnosis remains poorly characterized in real-world settings. We assessed its prognostic impact and the clinical features of patients with rPD in real-world de novo metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC).

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed 280 patients with de novo mCSPC who progressed to prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-defined CRPC from two multi-institutional cohorts: a conventional androgen deprivation therapy or combined androgen blockade (ADT/CAB) cohort (n = 223) and an upfront intensification cohort (n = 57). At CRPC diagnosis, patients were categorized as having PSA-only progression or PSA + rPD. Post-CRPC overall survival (OS) was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards models, while rPD-associated characteristics were examined using logistic regression.

Results

Patients with PSA + rPD had significantly shorter post-CRPC OS than those with PSA-only progression (ADT/CAB: 22 vs. 47 months, P < 0.001; upfront: 14 vs. 24 months, P = 0.010). Univariate Cox regression confirmed the adverse prognostic impact of rPD (hazard ratios, 2.11 [95% CI 1.39-3.21] and 2.43 [95% CI 1.20-4.96]). Lower baseline PSA levels were associated with rPD in both the ADT/CAB (odds ratio [OR], 0.65; 95% CI 0.42-0.99; P = 0.046) and upfront (OR, 0.29; 95% CI 0.12-0.71; P = 0.006) cohorts.

Conclusion

Radiographic progression at CRPC diagnosis predicts poor post-CRPC survival in real-world de novo mCSPC patients, regardless of initial treatment. Lower baseline PSA may be associated with rPD, although this exploratory finding requires validation. These findings support considering radiographic evaluation at CRPC diagnosis.

title: Nuclear eccentricity redistributes ultrasound-induced membrane tension in a three-dimensional tensegrity cell model.
abstract: Mechanosensitive channels respond to the local mechanical state of the cell membrane, but this spatial information is not captured by whole-cell averages. We used a three-dimensional acoustic-structure interaction model of a suspended spherical cell with a prestressed tensegrity cytoskeleton to examine how ultrasound frequency and nuclear position affect a strain-derived membrane-tension proxy. The nucleus was displaced by 0-6 μm, and 38 frequencies from 0.5 to 7.9 MHz were simulated at 10 kPa. All nuclear positions followed a similar whole-membrane frequency response. At 3.3 MHz, the area-weighted median ranged from 13.96 to 14.55 mN/m and P95 from 19.24 to 20.14 mN/m, whereas the P95 of the matched-location change reached 3.98-4.72 mN/m. At this frequency, nuclear eccentricity produced small, nonmonotonic changes in whole-membrane measures, with no consistent net increase despite local redistribution. Regions toward and opposite the nuclear displacement showed different local responses. Pressure changes from 1 to 20 kPa largely preserved spatial ordering at a fixed frequency, whereas different frequencies produced distinct membrane patterns. Threshold coverage depended on the strain-to-tension coefficient, and the volumetric-parameter and mesh analyses defined the numerical dependence of the result. These simulations identify nuclear position as a source of local membrane-loading differences under matched acoustic exposure, providing a mechanical hypothesis for spatially heterogeneous mechanotransduction.

title: Multimodal in vitro evaluation of experimentally induced enamel cracks before and after nano-hydroxyapatite application.
abstract: Dental enamel cracks are structural defects that may alter local morphology and provide confined sites for material deposition. Because mature enamel is acellular, spontaneous restoration of an established structural discontinuity is limited. Nano-hydroxyapatite (nHAp) has been investigated as a calcium-phosphate material, but its deposition within experimentally induced enamel cracks has not been comprehensively characterized across volumetric, chemical, and nanoscale endpoints. This in vitro study aimed to characterize structural, chemical, and nano-topographic changes associated with topical nHAp application to experimentally induced enamel cracks using complementary analytical modalities. Sixty sound human maxillary first premolars extracted for orthodontic treatment were thermally cycled (5-55 °C, 5000 cycles) to induce enamel cracks. The teeth were retained intact and allocated to three analytical cohorts (n = 20 per cohort): micro-computed tomography (µ-CT), Raman spectroscopy, and atomic force microscopy (AFM). Each specimen was examined with its assigned modality before and after standardized application of a 10 wt/vol% aqueous nHAp suspension. The primary outcome was the within-specimen change in apparent crack depth measured by µ-CT following nHAp application; because no comparator group was included, this quantity is a change over time within each specimen and not an effect attributable to nHAp. The eight remaining variables were secondary, exploratory endpoints, analyzed without adjustment for multiplicity. Paired comparisons were used for the pre- and post-application measurements. In the µ-CT cohort, mean apparent crack depth decreased from 156 ± 60 μm at baseline to 118 ± 78 μm after nHAp application (mean paired difference, - 38 μm, i.e., 24% of the baseline mean; P < 0.05), whereas enamel gray values showed no statistically significant change. Raman measurements showed higher post-application PO4-band intensity and crystallinity index and a lower CO3/PO4 ratio. AFM showed increased Sa, Sq, mean particle diameter, and surface coverage at the examined crack locations. Exact P values, 95% confidence intervals and paired effect sizes are not available for any endpoint (Sect. 2.8). Because the study lacked an untreated/vehicle control and did not chemically distinguish exogenous nHAp from newly formed endogenous mineral, these post-application changes are interpreted as deposition-associated structural and physicochemical modifications rather than definitive evidence of biological repair or de novo mineral formation; in a single-arm design they cannot be partitioned between the intervention and the concurrent storage, handling and re-imaging procedures. Topical nHAp application was associated with partial radiopaque occlusion of experimentally induced enamel cracks and marked changes in local mineral-associated Raman signals and surface nanotopography. The findings support further investigation of nHAp as a crack-occluding material but do not establish true remineralization, structural integration, long-term stability, or clinical efficacy. This in vitro study provides preliminary structural and physicochemical evidence that topical nHAp can modify experimentally induced enamel cracks. The findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require controlled studies with vehicle controls, direct mechanical and chemical durability testing, and clinical validation before therapeutic efficacy can be inferred.

title: VISION-GAN: Mask Conditioned U-Net GAN with Multi-Scale Auxiliary Supervision for Retinal Fundus Image Generation.
abstract: Retinal fundus imaging is essential for early detection of ocular and systemic disease, but training deep models is limited by data scarcity, privacy constraints, and class imbalance. Existing generative approaches mainly target global realism, with limited control over fine-grained retinal anatomy and lesion patterns. We address this by explicitly conditioning fundus image synthesis on retinal structural and lesion-specific priors. A multi-scale residual attention U-Net segments the blood vessels, optic disc, and exudates, and together with diabetic retinopathy (DR) severity labels are used as conditioning inputs to a mask-guided conditional GAN, effectively coupling discriminative segmentation with generative synthesis. The generator is a U-Net with a multi-path encoder and normalization-based conditioning (SPADE, AdaIN, and FiLM) in the decoder, enabling structural guidance, appearance variation, and disease-aware modulation, while a projection-based discriminator enforces local and global realism. The model is trained with a composite objective that combines hinge adversarial loss with multi-scale region-aware reconstruction and perceptual losses. We evaluate the framework on the APTOS, EyePACS, and Messidor-2 datasets using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), Kernel Inception Distance (KID), Inception Score (IS), Structural Similarity (SSIM), and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR). The proposed method achieves low FID, KID, and high SSIM, PSNR on all three datasets and improves the metrics over prior GAN-based fundus synthesis methods on Messidor-2. The downstream classification study performed showed that augmenting APTOS dataset with synthetic images improved ResNet-18 DR grading performance. These results show that anatomically conditioned synthesis from multi-mask priors yields realistic, diverse fundus images that are useful for mitigating data limitations in clinical deep learning.

title: Automated Severity Grading of Lumbar Spinal Stenosis on Sagittal MRI Using a Two-Stage Deep Learning Framework with External Clinical Validation.
abstract: Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) is a prevalent degenerative condition and a major cause of disability in aging populations. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the preferred modality for assessment; however, severity grading remains inconsistent across readers and institutions, limiting reproducibility and complicating clinical decision-making. This study presents LSS-Net, a two-stage deep learning framework for automated grading of central canal stenosis using sagittal T2-weighted MRI. The first stage performs vertebral localization using a single-stage object detector, enabling standardized extraction of intervertebral regions of interest. The second stage applies a Swin Transformer-based classifier to predict stenosis severity (Normal/Mild, Moderate, Severe). The framework was developed using a multi-center dataset of 1,975 studies and evaluated on a held-out subset. Vertebral localization achieved 97.9% F1-score, while severity classification reached a weighted F1-score of 77.1%. Performance was highest for Normal/Mild and Severe classes, with reduced accuracy observed in Moderate cases, reflecting known diagnostic ambiguity. External clinical validation was conducted on an independent dataset using two expert readers. The model demonstrated substantial agreement with a neurosurgeon (accuracy 75.1%, κ=0.73 ) and moderate agreement with a neuroradiologist (accuracy 51.0%, κ=0.56 ), with inter-expert agreement in a comparable range. These findings suggest that LSS-Net may support more consistent and reproducible LSS grading. However, performance limitations in borderline cases and the restricted use of single-slice sagittal input highlight the need for further validation and extension to multi-sequence and multi-compartment analysis before clinical deployment.

title: Active Learning and Cascaded nnU-Net v2 for Multi-structure Segmentation of Thoracic CT: A Single-Center Pilot Study.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of thoracic structures on chest computed tomography (CT) is important for lung cancer surgery, but manual annotation is labor intensive and particularly challenging for small structures such as pulmonary vessels and nodules. We compared four nnU-Net v2-based segmentation configurations: single-stage full-data training, active learning alone, cascaded segmentation alone, and active learning combined with cascaded segmentation in a retrospective single-center cohort. This retrospective study included chest CT scans from 85 patients. In the cascaded configurations, pulmonary lobes were segmented in the first stage to provide global anatomical context, followed by refinement of the bronchus, pulmonary vessels, and nodules within the constrained region. All four configurations were evaluated using the same fixed patient-level internal test set of 30 patients, with segmentation performance assessed using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and the 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95). The full-data baseline achieved DSCs of 0.92-0.93 for the five pulmonary lobes, with lower performance for the bronchus (0.82), pulmonary vessels (0.67), and pulmonary nodules (0.78). The combined active learning and cascaded configuration improved lobar DSCs to 0.94-0.96. Compared with the baseline, DSC increased to 0.90, 0.77, and 0.86 for the bronchus, pulmonary vessels, and pulmonary nodules, respectively (all p < 0.05), while HD95 decreased from 5.4 to 2.5 mm for pulmonary vessels and from 4.8 to 2.1 mm for pulmonary nodules. In this single-center cohort, cascaded segmentation strategies showed improved internal test performance for small thoracic structures, supporting further evaluation in larger multicenter cohorts.

title: Swin-DDM-Net: A Swin Transformer-Based Framework with Direction Difference Maps for Nuclear Instance Segmentation and Classification.
abstract: Accurate nuclear instance segmentation and classification are fundamental prerequisites for quantitative digital pathology, but automated analysis remains difficult because nuclei vary substantially in shape, size, staining, density, and class-specific morphology. Swin-DDM-Net combines a hierarchical Swin Transformer encoder with three task-specific decoder branches for nuclear foreground prediction, horizontal-vertical distance regression, and pixel-level nuclear classification. The predicted distance maps are transformed into a Direction Difference Map (DDM), which captures local direction discontinuities at touching nuclear boundaries and refines marker-controlled watershed segmentation. Experiments on six public histopathology patch datasets, including CoNSeP, Kumar, CPM-15, CPM-17, TNBC, and CRCHisto, show competitive instance segmentation, patch-level cross-domain generalization, and nuclear classification performance relative to classical tools, convolutional baselines, HoVer-Net, CDNet, CellViT, and Mudslide under the evaluated settings. The results support the value of combining Transformer-based contextual representation with explicit instance geometry for cell-level computational pathology. The method should be interpreted as benchmark-level algorithmic evidence; statistical uncertainty analysis, dataset-license confirmation, public code and weight release, and external whole-slide-image (WSI) validation remain necessary before clinical deployment.

title: DINOv3-SAM: Fusing Semantic and Anatomical Foundation Models for Robust Medical Image Classification.
abstract: Robust medical image classification remains a persistent challenge due to heterogeneous acquisition protocols, label noise, and subtle inter-class variability. In chest radiography, these difficulties are compounded by shortcut learning from non-anatomical artifacts and projection variability, which severely undermine generalization. To address these limitations, we propose DINOv3-SAM, a dual-encoder framework that synergistically integrates complementary visual representations. The architecture combines a self-supervised DINOv3 vision transformer, which captures global semantic context, with the Segment Anything Model (SAM) image encoder, which provides anatomy-aware spatial features. The two feature streams are spatially aligned and adaptively refined through a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), which emphasizes informative channels and diagnostically relevant regions prior to classification. Notably, only the final DINOv3 layers are fine-tuned while SAM remains frozen, yielding a computationally efficient framework with only 5.3 million trainable parameters. We evaluate DINOv3-SAM across five public datasets spanning diverse modalities and diagnostic tasks: pediatric pneumonia classification, cardiomegaly detection, large-scale RSNA pneumonia detection, COVID-19 radiography, and dermatological lesion classification. A unified stratified train/validation/test protocol ensures consistent and fair evaluation across both binary and multi-class settings. Each configuration was trained three times with different random seeds, and comprehensive comparisons against reproduced CNN baselines and published state-of-the-art methods, supported by statistical significance testing, demonstrate improvements across most datasets and metrics. The proposed framework achieves a mean accuracy of 94.94% (±3.06) on pediatric pneumonia, 97.24% (±0.77) accuracy (AUC 0.998 ±0.001) on COVID-19 radiography, and a mean AUC of 0.8705 (±0.0445) on the challenging RSNA benchmark. These results underscore the efficacy of fusing self-supervised semantic representations with segmentation-informed anatomical cues to enhance robustness against dataset bias, acquisition variability, and cross-domain shifts. The proposed approach offers a reliable foundation for multi-dataset and multi-modality medical image classification in research-oriented decision-support systems.

title: MDF-Net: A Decoupled Multimodal Fusion Network with Contrastive Learning for Reliable Brain Tumor Segmentation on Multi-sequence MRI.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of brain tumors from multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is critical for clinical diagnosis, treatment planning, and longitudinal disease monitoring. Multimodal MRI provides complementary information across sequences, yet this complementarity is entangled with substantial cross-modal redundancy. Prevailing coupled fusion schemes merge modalities into a single shared space, where discriminative tumor-specific cues and redundant shared content are blended indiscriminately, an effect further aggravated by cross-scale feature inconsistency and by the difficulty of delineating small enhancing lesions. To address these issues, we recast multimodal segmentation as a decoupled representation learning problem and propose a Multimodal Decoupled Fusion Network (MDF-Net) that explicitly disentangles the fused representation into complementary and non-redundant components. At its core, a Tri-Branch Decoupling (TBD) module separates the fused features into spatial, channel, and instance components, and a Feature Contrastive Learning (FCL) objective enforces their complementarity while suppressing inter-branch redundancy. To provide scale-aware and locally coherent features for decoupling, an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module and a Local Window Self-Attention (LWSA) module jointly model multi-scale context and local dependencies, while a dedicated Small Lesion Refinement (SLR) module improves the delineation of small and ambiguous enhancing tumors through multi-scale detection and boundary-aware refinement. Extensive experiments on two publicly available benchmarks, BraTS 2023 and FeTS 2022, demonstrate that MDF-Net achieves competitive and well-balanced performance relative to recent state-of-the-art methods across tumor sub-regions and multiple evaluation metrics, with particularly accurate whole-tumor boundary delineation. Ablation studies and feature-space visualizations further confirm that explicit decoupling yields a more structured embedding space and that each component makes a complementary contribution to segmentation performance.

title: Predictive Nomogram for High Ki-67 Expression using Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound of Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: Identifying reliable prognostic factors for clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is challenging, thereby complicating treatment and follow-up decisions. The aim of this study was to develop and validate a contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS)-based nomogram to predict high Ki-67 expression in ccRCC. This retrospective study analysed 312 patients from two centres (training, n = 212; validation, n = 100) who underwent preoperative CEUS. Postoperative pathology confirmed ccRCC. Immunohistochemistry assessed Ki-67 expression and CD34-positive microvascular density (CD34 + MVD). A nomogram was developed using multivariate logistic regression and validated based on the area under the curve (AUC). Predictive performance was compared with tumour-node-metastasis (TNM) staging and World Health Organisation/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) grading using the DeLong test. Spearman's correlation coefficients were compared among CD34 + MVD, WHO/ISUP grade, and Ki-67 expression. Significant predictors of high Ki-67 expression included tumour diameter ≥ 3.85 cm (odds ratio [OR]: 1.525, 95% confidence interval: 1.054-2.205), washout time ≤ 34.7 s (OR: 0.942, 95% Cl: 0.911-0.975), and necrosis ≥ 9.158% (OR: 1.105, 95% Cl: 1.021-1.195). The nomogram achieved an AUC of 0.858 (training set) and 0.810 (validation set), outperforming TNM staging (AUC: 0.733) and WHO/ISUP grading (AUC: 0.761). Ki-67 expression correlated negatively with CD34+MVD (r = -0.632) and positively with WHO/ISUP grading (r=0.620), whereas CD34+MVD expression was negatively correlated with WHO/ISUP grading (r = -0.607). The CEUS-based nomogram demonstrated superior predictive accuracy for high Ki-67 expression compared with TNM staging and WHO/ISUP grading, supporting its potential for personalised treatment and more precise follow-up surveillance programmes.

title: SPBA-Net: A Comparative Feature Enhancement Network for Midbrain Segmentation in Transcranial Sonography.
abstract: Segmentation of the midbrain during transcranial sonography is an essential step in the ultrasound evaluation of Parkinson's disease. However, this method is limited by issues such as low imaging resolution, unclear anatomical boundaries, and poor contrast between tissues. We propose a comparative feature enhancement network called SPBA-Net, which mitigates these shortcomings. The framework first employs a learnable butterfly-shaped prior guidance module (LSPG) to ensure anatomical consistency and embeds a gated boundary enhancement unit (BEA) in the decoder to reduce edge blurring. Furthermore, we introduce a sparse non-local attention mechanism (SNLA) and an adaptive multiscale fusion module (ASFM) to efficiently capture long-range feature dependencies. Finally, we design a dynamically gated reverse attention compensation module (DGRC) to address the foreground-background imbalance and integrate a composite multiscale loss function. In the midbrain segmentation task, SPBA-Net outperformed mainstream baseline models on all evaluation metrics, achieving a DSC of 0.9556 while maintaining reasonable computational overhead. In addition, this model is also applicable to segmentation tasks involving other objects and other modalities. This indicates that the proposed SPBA-Net not only facilitates automated quantitative analysis of the midbrain in the future but can also be transferred to other segmentation tasks.

title: Skull-Base Synthetic CT from Brain MRI: Development, Independent-Center Validation, and Radiologist Evaluation.
abstract: We developed and evaluated a deep learning pipeline for skull-base synthetic computed tomography (sCT) generation from routine non-contrast T1-weighted and T2-weighted brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), focusing on clinically relevant bony anatomy for neurosurgical and radiotherapy workflows. We retrospectively collected 184 manually registered T1/T2/CT triplets for training and internal validation (166/18 split) and 43 cases from a second center for independent-center validation. A three-dimensional Swin-UNETR generator was trained with bone-weighted multiscale reconstruction, perceptual, and adversarial losses. Two board-certified radiologists independently scored 16 skull-base structures, artifacts, and diagnostic acceptability on raw sCT in Hounsfield units (HU), without histogram matching; this blinded review was the primary endpoint. Acceptability was 76.7% for Rater 1 and 67.4% for Rater 2 (pooled 72.1%, cluster-robust 95% CI 58.5-82.6%), with mean structure scores from 2.67 to 4.85 out of 5. Raw sCT showed limited absolute HU calibration (global MAE 364±50 HU, bone Dice 0.38±0.09 ), with a compressed dynamic range in which air and soft tissue were overestimated and dense bone underestimated; histogram-matched outputs, reported as a secondary analysis, reached bone Dice 0.88±0.03 and bone MAE 26.31±5.03 HU. Halo artifacts were near-universal, and false-canal artifacts occurred in 21-30% of cases. The method shows promise as a radiation-free adjunct for skull-base visualization, but the present results do not support replacing dedicated CT for diagnostic, dosimetric, or physics-based applications.

title: Multi-task Model with​ Peritumoral MRI Radiomics Learning for Breast Cancer Segmentation-Guided Subtype Classification.
abstract: Accurate breast cancer molecular subtype classification is important for treatment planning, but immunohistochemical assessment may be affected by intratumoral heterogeneity and requires invasive tissue sampling. We hypothesize that segmentation-guided learning of tumor-core and peritumoral microenvironment (PTM) MRI features would improve molecular subtype discrimination over tumor-core-only analysis. A transformer-based segmentation network integrates cross-modal and multi-scale features to delineate tumors, after which the predicted masks are used to construct tumor-core and peritumoral inputs for an energy-regularized classification network. On the test cohort, the retrospective single-center study includes 381 patients with histopathologically confirmed breast cancer and corresponding DCE, DWI, T1WI, and T2WI images. The proposed method achieves a Dice coefficient of 88.29%, a Jaccard index of 79.80%, a precision of 91.98%, and a 95HD of 4.03 pixels for tumor segmentation. For molecular subtype classification, it achieves an accuracy of 84.0%, a macro-averaged sensitivity of 85.7%, a macro-averaged specificity of 94.8%, and a macro-averaged F1 score of 83.9%, providing the best overall performance among the evaluated methods. These findings support further evaluation of segmentation-guided multimodal MRI analysis for preoperative molecular subtype assessment.

title: Performance of Deep Learning Algorithms for Segmentation of Shoulder Anatomy on MRI: A Systematic Review.
abstract: To synthesize the performance and methodological characteristics of fully automated deep learning algorithms for shoulder magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) segmentation. This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. CENTRAL, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were searched from inception through July 17, 2026. The protocol specified fully automated deep learning-based pixel-wise segmentation of shoulder MRI, an expert-derived MRI-space reference standard, and quantitative segmentation metrics. Two reviewers independently screened records; unresolved disagreements were adjudicated by a senior reviewer. Overlapping datasets were linked during synthesis. Of 354 identified records, 169 duplicates were removed, 185 records were screened, and 53 full-text reports were assessed. Thirty-five reports were included (31 journal articles and 4 full conference papers; 2018-2026). U-Net-based encoder-decoder architectures predominated, with additional region-based, transformer, adversarial, and autoencoder approaches. Dice similarity coefficients ranged from approximately 0.81-0.99 for osseous targets, 0.71-0.99 for shoulder muscles, and 0.58-0.94 for tendon or tear regions; intersection-over-union values for tear or surgical-planning regions ranged from 0.45-0.83. MRI protocols and validation designs were heterogeneous, and most reports described retrospective single-center investigations. Five reports used independent external test sets; several others included multicenter images. Overlapping cohorts precluded a valid pooled participant count. Deep learning achieved high accuracy for shoulder bones and rotator-cuff muscles in selected datasets, whereas tear-region performance was more variable. Multicenter patient-level validation and standardized annotation and reporting are needed before routine clinical deployment.

title: ParetoRx: A Multiobjective Radiogenomic Framework Integrating Pareto Optimization and Q-Learning for Exploratory Compound Prioritization in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Imaging-defined high-risk phenotypes may capture biologically aggressive disease states, but translating them into therapeutic hypotheses remains challenging. We developed ParetoRx, a radiogenomic imaging-informatics framework integrating computed tomography radiomics, pathway-level transcriptomic analysis, multiobjective Pareto optimization, and model-free Q-learning for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Pretreatment CT data from 402 patients were used for model development and internal validation, with 110 patients forming a held-out external cohort. The final radiomics model achieved an external C-index of 0.707 (95% CI 0.627-0.783); high-risk patients had worse overall survival (HR 3.461, 95% CI 1.674-7.153), with minimal change after adjustment for histology (HR 3.444, 95% CI 1.662-7.137). Gene set enrichment and single-sample pathway analyses identified exploratory associations involving E2F targets, MYC targets V1, inflammatory response, and hypoxia, although no pathway met FDR < 0.05. LINCS L1000 perturbational profiles were evaluated using transcriptomic reversal, pathway specificity, and a feasibility-related proxy, with 4188 compounds retained in the common complete-case analysis. Multiobjective Pareto optimization was combined with three-split consensus ranking and sequential policy evaluation. TWS-119 showed consistent prioritization across all three splits (ranks 1, 3, and 4) and was Pareto-optimal in each split. In simulation-based evaluation, model-free Q-learning achieved higher terminal-goal attainment than myopic and static policies across all three splits, with improvements of approximately 6.2-13.3 percentage points over the myopic comparator. These findings support ParetoRx as an exploratory framework for biologically informed compound prioritization and computational sequential decision-making, while independent drug response and clinical validation remain necessary.

title: Benchmark Accuracy Does Not Transfer: Domain Adaptive Deep Learning for Diabetic Retinopathy Detection in a Bangladeshi Clinical Setting.
abstract: Deep learning could make diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening more accessible where ophthalmologists are scarce, but high benchmark accuracy does not guarantee reliable clinical performance. We investigate this gap using 3662 images from APTOS 2019 for source training and a balanced evaluation corpus of 500 fundus images (250 DR, 250 No-DR) from a Bangladeshi clinic, graded by a single experienced ophthalmologist. Source-trained models achieved 94.26-96.80% accuracy under tenfold cross-validation on APTOS, yet achieved only 49.4-50.6% (mean 50.0%) when applied directly to the clinical images. The resulting 44.46-46.85 percentage-point losses across all six architectures provide consistent quantitative evidence of severe domain shift. A full-cohort feature comparison yielded a classical-feature Fréchet distance of 133.49 and an MMD 2 of 0.3967 (permutation p=0.0005 ). To recover target-domain performance, we evaluate an adaptation pipeline that integrates retinal-specific preprocessing, progressive fine-tuning with discriminative learning rates, soft-voting inference, and test-time augmentation. Aggregated out-of-fold evaluation produced 81.0% accuracy (95% Wilson CI 77.3-84.2%), 70.0% sensitivity, 92.0% specificity, 89.7% precision, and a 78.7% F1 score. Fine-tuning increased mean individual-model accuracy by 27.1 percentage points, whereas preprocessing contributed a descriptive 2.0-point increase. These findings quantify a substantial benchmark-to-clinic gap and show that target-domain adaptation can improve performance, while the remaining false-negative rate and single-clinic design preclude claims of clinical readiness.

title: Diffusion Prior-Driven Vision-Language Adaptation for Few-Shot Medical Anomaly Detection.
abstract: Unsupervised medical anomaly detection faces dual challenges of pathological data scarcity and domain gaps when transferring general-purpose vision-language models to fine-grained tasks. This study aims to address the misalignment between global semantic representations and local pathological nuances by proposing a novel hybrid supervision framework. We propose a flexible vision-language adaptation framework in which diffusion-based pseudo-anomaly synthesis serves as an optional training enhancement. For CheXpert and BUSI, region-guided diffusion generates localized pseudo-anomalies to provide additional discriminative supervision. For BrainMRI, the framework is trained exclusively on normal reference images without any synthetic anomaly augmentation, allowing us to assess its effectiveness independently of the diffusion synthesis component. The architecture incorporates a local-enhanced feature rectifier to enhance local textural representation, a zero-initialized hypersphere-aligned residual adapter for stable cross-modal manifold alignment, and a temperature-scaled mapmaker for multi-scale dense anomaly localization. Performance was evaluated across three medical imaging modalities under multiple few-shot configurations. Our method remains highly competitive compared to state-of-the-art approaches in terms of image-level detection and pixel-level localization. On the ultrasound dataset under a 32-shot setting, the framework achieved an image-level area under the curve of 94.2% and a pixel-level area under the curve of 96.6%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework across the evaluated medical imaging modalities under different training configurations. In particular, its competitive performance on BrainMRI without synthetic anomaly augmentation suggests that the vision-language adaptation framework can remain effective when offline pseudo-anomaly generation is unavailable. The code involved in this study is publicly available on website https://github.com/SWLee777/DiffVLA .

title: Propagation of Low-Dose-Induced Noise Characteristics Across Deep Learning Layers in CT Imaging.
abstract: Dose reduction in computed tomography (CT) imaging impacts diagnostic accuracy for human observers and potentially artificial intelligence (AI) systems. As noise propagates through an AI model, its characteristics change, possibly influencing model performance. This study aims to develop a configurable low-dose CT simulation tool in image-space and analyze noise behavior in deep learning (DL) layers. The noise characteristics were quantified using the noise power spectrum (NPS) within homogeneous phantom regions. NPS area under the curve (intensity) and median frequency (texture) were reported. Low-dose CT images were simulated using a custom program that was calibrated for configurable noise intensity and texture. Noise was generated at texture levels. Pre-trained U-Net features were extracted from reference and simulated low-dose images, enabling NPS-based analysis of noise propagation across deep learning layers. NPS from simulated low-dose CT images matched reference NPS for various intensity and texture values. Feature analysis revealed progressive convergence of noise characteristics across deep learning layers, with batch normalization mitigating amplification observed after convolution and ReLU activation. Differences in noise texture between low-dose simulations converge along the U-Net contracting path. The image-space simulation tool offers a viable alternative for researchers lacking access to raw data, supporting future AI-focused dose optimization studies. However, whether these outcomes translate to segmentation performance remains unclear and warrants further investigation.

title: EDGE-Net: Enhanced Distribution Gated Eye-Vessel Network for Ophthalmic Vascular Segmentation with Topological Constraints.
abstract: Ophthalmic vascular segmentation supports quantitative analysis of the retinal vasculature, yet thin vessels, low contrast, and complex vascular topology remain challenging. We propose EDGE-Net (Enhanced Distribution Gated Eye-vessel Network), which combines the CLARITY preprocessing pipeline, a Dynamic Dual-Stream Attention Block (DDSAB), Multi-Stream Gated Feature Fusion (MSGFF), and topology-aware loss terms based on persistent homology and connectivity regularization. The framework is evaluated on three retinal vessel datasets (DRIVE, CHASE_DB1, and STARE) and two coronary angiography datasets (DCA1 and CHUAC); all hyperparameters are selected on a DRIVE validation split and then fixed for every dataset. EDGE-Net obtains the highest F1 score on all five datasets, ranging from 0.8394 to 0.8456 on the retinal datasets and from 0.7421 to 0.7518 on the coronary datasets, although it does not achieve the highest accuracy or specificity on every dataset. When the same dual-threshold iterative (DTI) post-processing is applied to every method on DRIVE, EDGE-Net obtains the lowest Vessel Connectivity Assessment score (3.31 versus 3.58 for the strongest competitor) and the highest Junction Preservation Rate (0.842 versus 0.812); both differences are significant after Holm correction (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.01 ). A controlled ablation attributes most of the pixel-level gain to DDSAB and MSGFF and most of the junction-preservation gain to the topology loss. Potential downstream uses include anatomically plausible vascular-network analysis; direct clinical benefit is not evaluated in this study.

title: Diagnostic Performance and Calibration of AI Models for Thyroid Ultrasound Malignancy Classification: From TN5000 to ThyroidXL.
abstract: We evaluated cross-dataset transportability of three frozen encoders for binary benign-versus-malignant thyroid ultrasound classification using expert-defined nodule regions and one external cohort. Logistic regression classifiers using DINOv2, TinyUSFM, and ResNet18 features were developed on 3500 TN5000 images, calibrated on 477 duplicate-clean validation images and tested on 958 images. External evaluation used maximum image scores from 2083 ThyroidXL images in 739 patients with cytological or histopathological outcomes. No external retraining, recalibration or threshold adjustment was performed. Additional analyses evaluated four classifiers, encoder-recommended preprocessing and calibration intercepts and slopes. Internal areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were 0.9081 for TinyUSFM, 0.8946 for DINOv2, and 0.8896 for ResNet18. Primary external AUROCs were 0.8464 (95% confidence interval, 0.8164-0.8731), 0.7954, and 0.7833, respectively. Sensitivities at frozen high-sensitivity thresholds were 0.9972, 0.9717, and 0.9887, but specificities were 0.1736, 0.1891, and 0.1373. External calibration intercepts were negative; slopes were 0.891, 0.645, and 0.697. DINOv2 ranked first externally with four of five classifiers. With recommended preprocessing, ResNet18 ranked first numerically (0.8329 versus 0.8214 for DINOv2); their paired difference was inconclusive. Encoder rankings depended on the classifier and preprocessing. These results apply to the three evaluated implementations, not pretraining strategies generally. Transported patient scores overestimated malignancy and had low specificity. Prospective assessment is needed before clinical use.

title: Critical Validation of Deep Learning-Based Cervical Vertebral Fracture Detection on Computed Tomography Localizer Radiographs.
abstract: Localizer radiographs are low-resolution two-dimensional overview images acquired prior to computed tomography (CT) scans. Their automated analysis could support the early detection of cervical vertebral fractures in trauma patients and thus enable immediate adjustment of imaging protocols. This study investigated to what extent deep learning-based methods can reliably detect such fractures on localizer radiographs, with a focus on critically validating model behavior beyond standard performance metrics. On a custom-annotated dataset of 346 trauma patients, two approaches were compared: a full-image binary classification and a two-step pipeline that first localizes the cervical spine and then classifies the cropped region. Model validity was assessed through a permutation test, occlusion testing, gradient-weighted class activation mapping, an analysis of potential confounders, and a subgroup analysis by anatomical fracture location. The full-image classifier formally achieved the highest test-set performance with a precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 0.477, compared with 0.349 for the cervical-spine-level classifier. Our validity analysis indicates that the full-image classifier does not primarily rely on the fracture region itself, rendering it unsuitable for clinical use. This work therefore presents a case study of shortcut learning and illustrates validation methods that may be of value for comparable studies on small datasets with visually subtle targets.

title: The Deep Learning-Based Prediction Method for Cervical Lymph Node Metastasis of Thyroid Cancer Based on Multimodal Data.
abstract: Thyroid cancer is a common malignant tumor worldwide, and there is a risk of misdiagnosis or over-treatment for small-sized thyroid cancer. The key to eliminating this risk lies in predicting cervical lymph node metastasis. The traditional manual prediction methods are not ideal, so this paper proposes an intelligent prediction method based on deep learning. This method is based on common clinical examination data, including ultrasound images, ultrasound image text descriptions, and blood test data. A deep convolutional neural network model is proposed using data from these three modalities as inputs. The model integrates multimodal data features through mean cross-attention and extracts fine-grained classification information from the fused feature map through a bilinear CNN network, demonstrating strong feature discrimination ability. Through collecting data and conducting various experiments, the experimental results show that the model proposed in this paper has good performance in predicting cervical lymph node metastasis, is better than the manual prediction, and has broad application prospects. Future research will continue to strive for data collection, increasing the amount of collected data and improving multi-center representativeness, and enhancing the diagnostic and predictive capabilities of the network model through technological improvements.

title: Learnable Pixel-Level Reward Modeling and Pixel-Wise Probability Mixing for Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation.
abstract: In semi-supervised medical image segmentation, pseudo-labeling and data mixing are widely adopted to leverage unlabeled images, yet conventional methods suffer from coarse-grained operations. Specifically, global filtering strategies typically rely on heuristic confidence scores that may not accurately reflect local pseudo-label reliability and apply spatially uniform loss weights to all pixels within retained samples, failing to reliably evaluate and accommodate spatial quality variations within pseudo-labels. Meanwhile, coarse-grained region-level mixing violently disrupts the inherent continuity of anatomical structures, frequently introducing severe semantic mismatches and misleading boundary targets during training. To address these limitations, we propose a semi-supervised segmentation framework based on learnable pixel-level reward modeling and pixel-wise probability mixing. A data-driven pixel-level reward map is constructed to provide learnable pixel-level reliability estimation instead of relying solely on heuristic confidence scores. These continuous reward scores are directly converted into fine-grained pixel-wise loss weights, dynamically regulating each pixel's optimization contribution rather than relying on hard confidence-based sample filtering; an empty-foreground safeguard only suppresses degenerate unlabeled samples with negligible predicted foreground. Furthermore, local pseudo-label distributions are adaptively refined via pixel-wise probability mixing within the continuous class probability space. This mechanism softly fuses the probability distributions of low-reward pixels with those of semantically consistent high-reward donor pixels, successfully bypassing the structural constraints of region-level mixing. Extensive experiments on the ACDC, BUSI, and Synapse datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive semi-supervised baselines under limited labeled-data settings.

title: Feasibility of Simulated Low-Dose CT with Deep Learning Denoising for Lymphoma PET/CT Imaging: A Clinical Study on Lesion Detection, Staging, and Therapy Response.
abstract: [18F] FDG PET/CT is central to lymphoma staging and treatment-response assessment, but repeated examinations increase cumulative radiation exposure, largely from the CT component. This retrospective study included 152 patients with 211 whole-body PET/CT scans and evaluated whether deep learning-denoised simulated low-dose CT can preserve diagnostic performance. A single-scan cohort of 108 patients was used exclusively for model development, while an independent follow-up cohort of 44 patients (103 examinations) was reserved for quantitative evaluation and a fully crossed multi-reader, multi-case study. Simulated low-dose CT images ranging from 2/3 to 1/8 of the standard dose were reviewed, and the 1/4-dose level was selected as the lowest clinically acceptable level. A denoising model was trained using paired standard-dose CT (SDCT) and simulated low-dose CT at 1/4 of the standard dose (SLDCT) images. Six nuclear medicine physicians evaluated three imaging conditions: PET/CT with SDCT, PET/CT with SLDCT, and PET/CT with denoised SLDCT (D-SLDCT), for image quality, lesion detectability, staging, and treatment response. D-SLDCT significantly improved quantitative image quality compared with SLDCT (all p < 0.0001) and increased subjective image-quality scores (4.11 ± 0.46 vs 3.00 ± 0.00). Staging accuracy was lower under the SLDCT condition than under the SDCT condition (MAE, 1.50 ± 0.27 vs 1.40 ± 0.20; p = 0.0011), whereas the D-SLDCT condition did not differ significantly from the SDCT condition (MAE, 1.44 ± 0.22; p = 0.47). Differences were more pronounced in patients with BMI ≥ 24 kg/m 2 and among junior readers. Lesion detectability and treatment-response assessment did not differ significantly across conditions, while within-reader lesion-detection agreement with the SDCT condition improved after denoising (κ = 0.72 vs 0.67). The D-SLDCT condition preserved diagnostic performance, supporting radiation-conscious lymphoma PET/CT. This study was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR) on February 14, 2026 (registration number: ChiCTR2600119037).

title: Nondisease Sources of Radiomic Texture Variation on Plain Radiographs: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Anatomical Region, Projection, and Resolution in a Public Fracture Archive.
abstract: Radiomic texture features from plain radiographs feed machine learning models on the assumption that they reflect tissue rather than anatomy or acquisition. In a public multihospital fracture archive, we quantified how anatomical region and radiographic projection, each adjusted for the other and for image resolution, shift 17 radiomic features, how much feature variance resolution explains, and a bony superimposition contrast defined within region. This retrospective cross-sectional secondary analysis used FracAtlas (4083 musculoskeletal radiographs from three hospitals); 4024 images were analyzed. For each z-scored feature (10 first-order, 7 Gy-level co-occurrence matrix [GLCM]), linear models estimated adjusted differences (β, SD units), and resolution by variance explained (R 2 ), with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction within each factor. Superimposition (hip and shoulder vs hand and leg; n = 3630), a grouping of regions, was analyzed as a pooled regional contrast rather than an independent factor. Region shifted 16 of 17 features (radiomic uniformity, hand vs leg - 0.66 SD [95% CI - 0.72 to - 0.59]). Resolution explained up to 16.8% of single-feature variance and changed the fracture log-odds coefficient by more than 15% for 7 of 10 interpretable features. Projection had the smallest effects (radiomic 10th percentile, lateral vs frontal - 0.32 SD). The superimposition contrast produced the largest shifts (GLCM energy - 2.26 SD [95% CI - 2.36 to - 2.16]). Radiomic texture on plain radiographs varies substantially with anatomy and acquisition, independently of fracture status. Radiograph radiomics studies should record and adjust for region, projection, and resolution, report region-specific estimates, and validate across sites.
